So I thought it necessary to urge the brothers to go on ahead to you and arrange in advance for the gift you have promised, so that it may be ready as a willing gift, not as an exaction.

Here is the reason for all the arranging, and it turns on two words held deliberately apart.

A willing gift is, in the Greek, a blessing — eulogia, the word that gives us eulogy, meaning a good word spoken, and by extension a benefit freely bestowed. That is what Paul wants the money to be: a blessing, given as blessings are given.

Not as an exaction is pleonexia — greed, covetousness, the grasping that takes what is not freely offered. It is a hard word, and Paul uses it of what the collection would become if it were extracted rather than given. The same root turned up at 2:11 of Satan getting the better of someone in a transaction.

So the same sum of money, arriving in the same bag on the same day, is either a blessing or a shakedown, and the difference is not in the amount. It is in whether it was freely given.

That should be allowed to land on how churches actually raise money, because the mechanisms that produce compulsion are rarely crude. Nobody is threatened. But there is the giving made visible so that the level is known; the target announced with a thermometer on the wall; the appeal placed at the emotional peak of a meeting; the pledge card passed along a row where everyone can see who is filling one in; the quiet awareness that the treasurer knows. All of these work. All of them shift the reason a person gives from what is in his heart to what the room expects.

Paul’s instinct is to build the structure that makes freedom possible: give people notice, give them time, let them decide at home, and arrange to be absent while they do it. That is what arrange in advance means here. He is not making it easier to give; he is making it possible to give freely.

And notice what he assumes about God in all this. He is prepared to risk a smaller collection in order to have a genuine one. He evidently does not believe that God needs the money badly enough to accept it on any terms — which is exactly right, since the whole letter has been saying that the God in question owns everything and became poor on purpose.

There is a personal version of the same test. Before you give, it is worth knowing which sentence you are answering: “I want to,” or “I would look bad if I did not.” The second is not wicked, and God is not standing over anybody with a stopwatch. But Paul has gone to considerable trouble here to make sure the Corinthians could answer the first.

verseByVerse.quote: The point is this: whoever sows sparingly will also reap sparingly, and whoever sows bountifully will also reap bountifully.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The point is this: whoever sows sparingly will also reap sparingly, and whoever sows bountifully will also reap bountifully.

Now the principle, and it is drawn from the one place everybody in the ancient world understood.

Stage it. A farmer walks out in autumn with a bag of seed and a decision to make, and the decision is genuinely painful, because the seed in that bag is food. He could eat it. His family can see it. And what he is being asked to do is throw it on the ground and cover it up, where it will do nobody any good for months. The more he keeps back to eat, the less goes into the ground, and the less comes up in the spring. Everyone farming knows this and it never stops being hard, because the eating is now and the harvest is later.

Giving works the same way, Paul says. What you release is not lost; it is planted. And the size of what comes back corresponds to what went in.

Now this verse must be handled carefully, because it has been made the foundation of one of the ugliest distortions of Christianity there is. The prosperity teacher quotes it and stops: sow generously into this ministry and God will return it to you multiplied, and the more you give the wealthier you will become. Money is thereby extracted from poor people by a promise God has not made, using a verse from a passage whose entire concern is that giving must not be extracted.

Three things in the passage itself take that reading apart, and none of them requires going outside the chapter.

First, look at what Paul actually says the harvest is. Not money. Verse 10 calls it the harvest of your righteousness. Verse 11 says you are enriched to be generous in every way. Verse 12 says the yield is thanksgivings to God. The crop, named three times, is righteousness, further generosity, and worship.

Second, the supply in verse 10 is seed to the sower and bread for food — enough to live on and enough to give again. That is provision for a farmer, not a fortune.

Third, and most decisively, the man Paul has just held up as the supreme example of generosity in 8:9 became poor. If sowing bountifully guaranteed material return, the Lord Jesus Christ is the counter-example, and so is Paul, who knew hunger and thirst, often without food (11:27).

What the verse does promise is real, and it is better than money. Nothing given away in God’s name is lost. It is seed in the ground, and there is a harvest attached to it that you will see. The only question the verse puts is the farmer’s question, and it is a hard one every autumn: how much are you willing to put out of your own reach, on the word of God that the ground is not a hole but a field?

parallels.desc: one gives freely, yet grows all the richer

verseByVerse.quote: Each one must give as he has decided in his heart, not reluctantly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Each one must give as he has decided in his heart, not reluctantly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver.

One verse, and it settles the manner, the method and the motive of Christian giving.

Each one. Not the wealthy, not those who feel able. Everybody. There is no exemption here for the poor, which is why the Macedonians gave out of the depths.

As he has decided in his heart. The verb means to purpose, to determine beforehand — a settled decision, made in advance, not a reaction. This is the strongest argument in Scripture for planned giving. It is a decision reached in private, with the figures in front of you, before any appeal is heard — and once made, it takes the question out of the offering plate and out of the emotional temperature of a meeting. Paul told this same church to do it weekly and in advance, so that there will be no collecting when I come (1 Cor. 16:2).

Then the two things it must not be, and both are shrewdly chosen.

Not reluctantly — literally, not out of grief. Not with a pang. That is the giving that is genuinely done and quietly resented, and the resentment usually surfaces later as a complaint about how the money is spent.

Not under compulsion — not because you had to. The pressure need not come from outside; most of it does not. It is the calculation of what is expected, what others will think, what a person in your position ought to be seen to do.

And then the sentence itself, and the word behind cheerful is a delight: hilaros, the root of our word hilarious. Paul had it from the Greek version of Proverbs. It is not sober approval; it is something closer to laughter. God loves a giver whose giving is a pleasure to him.

Which is a genuinely startling thing to be told, because it means God is not primarily after the money. He owns the cattle on a thousand hills and has no shortage (Ps. 50:10). What he loves is a particular kind of person: one for whom letting go has become a joy rather than a loss.

And that cannot be produced by trying. You cannot decide to find giving delightful, any more than you can decide to find a person attractive. It comes from somewhere else — from having grasped, somewhere below the level of argument, that you cannot out-give the one who has already given you everything, and that nothing you release was ever really at risk.

So if giving is currently a duty you perform with a small internal wince, the answer is not to give more grimly. It is to go back and look again at 8:9 until the arithmetic changes. Cheerful givers are made by contemplation, not by resolve.

parallels.desc: from every man whose heart moves him
the Greek Old Testament adds a line about God blessing a cheerful giver

verseByVerse.quote: And God is able to make all grace abound to you, so that having all sufficiency in all things at all times, you may abound in every good work.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And God is able to make all grace abound to you, so that having all sufficiency in all things at all times, you may abound in every good work.

Paul now supplies the reason a person can afford to give freely, and the sentence is built out of totality. Count the words: all grace, all sufficiency, all things, all times, every good work. Five in one line. He is piling them up on purpose.

Begin where he begins: God is able. That is the ground of the whole thing. Not “God will make you comfortable,” but God is able — the question of capacity is settled, and it is his capacity, not yours.

To make all grace abound to you. Grace again, the word running through both chapters. And here it plainly includes the material, since the context is money; but it is not only material, and Paul’s vocabulary refuses to let it shrink to that.

Then the key word: sufficiency. The Greek is autarkeia, and it has a history worth knowing. It was a great word among the Stoic philosophers, and it meant self-sufficiency — the ideal of the wise man who has trained himself to need nothing from anyone, and is therefore untouchable. It was an admirable and rather cold aspiration, and it depended entirely on the strength of the individual.

Paul takes the word and quietly turns it inside out. The Christian has autarkeia — he lacks nothing — and it does not come from within him at all. It is supplied. He is not self-sufficient; he is God-sufficient, and therefore has the freedom the Stoic wanted without the self-reliance the Stoic required. Paul says elsewhere that he has learned this by experience in both directions: I have learned in whatever situation I am to be content (Phil. 4:11), a sentence written from prison by a man who had been both well fed and hungry.

And then the purpose clause, which is the part that gets left out when this verse is quoted on its own. Why does God supply all sufficiency at all times? So that you may abound in every good work.

Not so that you may be secure. Not so that you may relax. The sufficiency is given to free the hands. God keeps a giver supplied for the same reason a farmer is kept in seed — because there is more sowing to do.

Which turns the verse into a genuine and searching question about what you have. Everyone has some margin, however small: the money, the time, the room, the skill, the years. The verse says that the margin was supplied, and it names the purpose it was supplied for. If it has been quietly reclassified as security, something has gone wrong in the accounting — because a God who gives seed and gets no crop has not been dealt with honestly.

verseByVerse.quote: As it is written, “He has distributed freely, he has given to the poor; his righteousness endures forever.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
As it is written, “He has distributed freely, he has given to the poor; his righteousness endures forever.”

Paul reaches for a psalm, and the choice repays looking up.

It is Psalm 112, and the whole psalm is a portrait of a particular kind of man: the one who fears the LORD. It describes him as gracious, merciful, unafraid of bad news, steady when others panic — and right in the middle of the portrait, as one of the marks of the God-fearing man, is this: he has distributed freely, he has given to the poor.

Which is worth noticing before anything else. In the psalmist’s picture of a godly life, open-handedness is not an optional extra for those of a generous temperament. It is one of the identifying features, listed alongside faith and courage as part of the description.

The verb behind distributed freely is a scattering word — the same motion as the farmer in verse 6, arm out, seed flung wide. It is not careful measured allocation. It is broadcast.

Then the phrase Paul is really after: his righteousness endures forever.

What does that mean? In the psalm it is the man’s own righteousness — his standing as a God-fearing man, his settled character, and specifically the fact that it does not fade. And the point Paul draws from it is the contrast running through this whole chapter. The money went out and is gone; nobody can now point to it. What it produced does not go anywhere. The righteousness endures.

Hold that against the fate of everything else a person accumulates. The savings will be spent by somebody. The house will belong to strangers. The estate will be divided and, within two generations, forgotten. Every pound kept is a pound that will eventually be lost, because that is the nature of what can be held. The only portion that survives is the portion that was given away — which is precisely what the Lord said when he told his disciples to lay up treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust destroys and where thieves do not break in and steal (Matt. 6:20).

And there is a further note, sounding under the psalm. The description of the man who scatters freely and whose righteousness endures forever is, in the end, the description of only one person perfectly. The whole psalm is a portrait of a life nobody has quite lived — except the one who gave to the poor to the point of having nothing, and whose righteousness endures forever because it is the righteousness of God himself. Every generous believer is a small copy of him, and the original is what the psalm was reaching for.

parallels.desc: he has distributed freely; he has given to the poor

verseByVerse.quote: He who supplies seed to the sower and bread for food will supply and multiply your seed for sowing and increase the harvest of your righteousness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He who supplies seed to the sower and bread for food will supply and multiply your seed for sowing and increase the harvest of your righteousness.

This is the verse that decides how verse 6 must be read, and it is the one the prosperity preacher never reaches.

Start with the two things God supplies, because Paul distinguishes them deliberately.

Seed to the sower — what is given to be put back in the ground. Bread for food — what is given to be eaten. Every farmer knows the difference and keeps the two in separate sacks, because confusing them is ruinous in both directions. Eat the seed and there is no crop next year. Sow the bread and the family starves this winter.

So God gives his people both, and the distinction is a mercy in two directions. It means you are meant to eat. Nothing in this passage requires a Christian to give away everything he has and call the resulting destitution faith; God supplies bread for food, deliberately, and it is his provision, not a compromise. And it means some of what you have was never meant for consumption. It is seed, and seed kept in the sack does nothing at all.

Then the two things he promises to do with it: supply and multiply your seed for sowing. Not multiply your bread. The increase is on the sowing side of the ledger. God takes a generous man and makes him more able to give, which is exactly what verse 8 said and exactly what most of us would not have chosen if asked.

And then the crop is named, and it is the plainest statement in the chapter: increase the harvest of your righteousness.

Not the harvest of your prosperity. Not your comfort, your security, your standard of living. Righteousness — the yield is a life more conformed to God, more like the man of Psalm 112, more like the Lord who became poor.

So the promise attached to generous giving in this chapter is exactly this: God will keep you supplied, he will enlarge your capacity to give, and he will make you a better man. That is the whole offer. It is enormously generous and it is not what is advertised on certain kinds of religious television, and the difference has cost poor and desperate people a great deal of money.

It is worth noticing the tenderness in the picture as well as the challenge. God is described as he who supplies seed to the sower — the one who fills the bag before the man walks out to the field. Nobody in this arrangement is being asked to generate anything. The seed you scatter was put in your hand, the bread you eat was put on your table, and the harvest is grown by someone else entirely. The farmer’s only part is the throwing.

parallels.desc: seed to the sower and bread to the eater

verseByVerse.quote: You will be enriched in every way to be generous in every way, which through us will produce thanksgiving to God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You will be enriched in every way to be generous in every way, which through us will produce thanksgiving to God.

The sentence has a hinge in the middle of it, and everything depends on reading past the hinge.

You will be enriched in every way. Stop there and it is a prosperity verse. Half of one, anyway — and half is exactly how it is usually quoted.

To be generous in every way. That is the purpose, and it is the third time in four verses Paul has attached the same clause to the same promise: sufficiency so that you may abound in good works (v. 8); seed multiplied for sowing (v. 10); enriched to be generous (v. 11). He will not let the promise stand on its own for a single sentence.

Take the picture behind it. A river is enriched by rainfall in the hills. It does not thereby become a lake. It becomes a river with more water going through it, and everything downstream is better for the rain that fell three counties away. Water that stops moving is not a richer river; it is a marsh, and it goes bad.

That is the theology of Christian prosperity in one image, and it explains why the New Testament is so unembarrassed about God giving people more. There is nothing wrong with increase. The question is only ever whether it is passing through.

Which puts an honest question to anyone whose circumstances have improved over the years — and most people’s do, quietly, without any single moment of becoming better off. Look at what happened to the increase. Almost always it was absorbed: a slightly larger house, a better car, a standard of living that rose to meet the income without a decision ever being taken. And the giving stayed roughly where it was when the income was half what it is now.

Nobody chose that. It happens by default, which is why it needs naming. The only reliable guard against it is the deciding of verse 7 — settling the proportion in advance, and revisiting it whenever the circumstances change, so that increase is a matter of policy rather than drift.

Then the end of the sentence, and it is where the whole chapter has been heading: which through us will produce thanksgiving to God. Follow the chain. God enriches the Corinthians. The Corinthians give. Paul and his companions carry it. Believers in Jerusalem receive it. And what comes out at the far end is not merely full stomachs. It is thanksgiving, going back up to the God who started it.

The money makes a complete circuit and returns to its source as worship. That is what your giving is actually doing, and most of it happens where you cannot see it.

verseByVerse.quote: For the ministry of this service is not only supplying the needs of the saints but is also overflowing in many thanksgivings to God. By their approval of this service, they will glorify God because of your submission that comes from your confession of the gospel of Christ, and the generosity of your contribution for them and for all others,
verseByVerse.commentary:
For the ministry of this service is not only supplying the needs of the saints but is also overflowing in many thanksgivings to God. By their approval of this service, they will glorify God because of your submission that comes from your confession of the gospel of Christ, and the generosity of your contribution for them and for all others,

Paul now spells out what a charitable collection actually accomplishes, and the list runs further than anyone would expect.

Not only supplying the needs of the saints. That much is obvious and it is real — people in Judea were hungry and this money bought food. Paul never sneers at the practical. But he says it is the smaller half.

But is also overflowing in many thanksgivings to God. The verb is the overflow word again. The gift does not stop when the need is met; it spills over into worship.

Then verse 13, which requires knowing what was actually at stake, because otherwise it reads as pious padding.

The deepest fracture in the first-century church was not doctrinal in the abstract. It was between Jewish believers in Jerusalem and Gentile believers in cities like Corinth. The Jewish Christians had watched a Law-free gospel spread among people who ate what they liked and had never been circumcised, and many of them were not at all sure about it. There had been a council about it (Acts 15). There had been a confrontation between Peter and Paul at Antioch (Gal. 2:11–14). The suspicion was mutual and it was serious.

Now picture what arrives. A bag of money, gathered over a year by Greek believers who have never seen Jerusalem, carried some eight hundred miles at real risk, for Jewish Christians they will never meet.

And Paul says what it will produce: they will glorify God because of your submission that comes from your confession of the gospel of Christ. The gift is evidence. It proves that the confession these Gentiles make is not words — that the gospel has actually gone in and changed what they do with their money. The Jerusalem believers will look at it and conclude that God is genuinely at work among the nations, and they will praise him for it.

So the collection is doing something no argument could do. Paul had made the case for Gentile inclusion at length and in person, and arguments do not dissolve suspicion. Sacrificial generosity does. It is very difficult to go on doubting the faith of people who have gone hungry so that you could eat.

Which is worth carrying into every division a church knows — between generations, between congregations, between believers who are wary of one another for reasons that are half real and half inherited. Suspicion is rarely argued away. It is dissolved by somebody being unmistakably and expensively kind, and Paul spent years of his life organising exactly that.

verseByVerse.quote: while they long for you and pray for you, because of the surpassing grace of God upon you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
while they long for you and pray for you, because of the surpassing grace of God upon you.

The last thing the money produces, and it is the loveliest.

They long for you. The word is a strong one — yearning, an ache of affection. And it belongs to Jewish believers in Jerusalem, directed toward Greek strangers in Corinth. These are the two groups whose relationship had been the great unresolved strain in the early church, and Paul expects the outcome of a collection to be homesickness for one another.

And pray for you. The people who received the money will spend themselves on the people who sent it. That is what happens when a gift is received rightly; it creates an obligation of love that has no way to discharge itself except in prayer.

Follow what has now happened to a sum of money. It fed the hungry. It produced thanksgiving to God. It proved the reality of a gospel that had been doubted. It bound two suspicious communities together. And it has set a group of people praying for another group by name, whom they will never meet in this life.

No accountant could show any of that on a statement. It is worth remembering when the giving feels like a transaction — a standing order leaving an account on the same day each month, with nothing visibly happening. Paul’s account of what money does in the kingdom is that most of its effects occur where the giver cannot see them and would not recognise them if he could.

Then the reason for their longing, and it is not what we would have written: because of the surpassing grace of God upon you.

Not “because of your generosity.” Not “because of your kindness.” The Jerusalem believers look at what the Corinthians have done and see straight past them to God. They do not end up admiring Corinth. They end up amazed at grace.

That is the mark of everything genuinely Christian, and it is the test that separates it from philanthropy. Philanthropy leaves people impressed with the giver, which is why the names go on the buildings. Grace leaves people looking at God, and the giver is not diminished by it — he is simply out of the way, which is the position every clay jar was designed to occupy (4:7).

And notice the word surpassing — grace beyond measure, exceeding the bounds. The observers in Jerusalem were not looking at a well-run appeal. They were looking at a phenomenon they could not account for on any human basis, and the only explanation big enough was God.

verseByVerse.quote: Thanks be to God for his inexpressible gift!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Thanks be to God for his inexpressible gift!

Two chapters about money end in an exclamation.

Paul has been organising a collection: timetables, delegates, audits, appeals, proportions, the risk to his own reputation. And at the end of it he does not summarise. He breaks off, as though he has looked up from the ledger and seen something.

The word is anekdiēgētos — un-out-narratable. It is built from a verb meaning to describe a thing all the way through, and Paul negates it. This is a gift that cannot be narrated to the end. Not that it is vague; the opposite. It is so definite and so large that language runs out before the description does.

What is the gift? He has already told us, in the previous chapter, and the two chapters have been standing on it the whole time: though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor (8:9). The gift is Christ.

Which makes this the proper end of everything Paul has said about generosity. He has given the Corinthians a great deal of instruction — decide in your heart, do it in advance, give proportionately, do not be pressured, finish what you started, keep the accounts clean. All of it is useful and none of it is the engine. The engine is that God gave his Son, and that no one has ever got to the end of describing it.

Stop and try. Begin anywhere — the Word who was with God and was God, born in a stable; the hands that made the world learning a trade; the one who had never been refused anything being refused a bed, a hearing, a friend. Follow it to the garden, and the whipping post, and the nails, and the darkness at noon, and the cry of a Son who had never been out of his Father’s sight. Then the morning, and the stone rolled away, and the wounds still in his hands so that they could be touched.

Now add what it purchased: a debt cancelled that could never have been paid; enemies made sons and daughters; the Spirit of God taking up residence in ordinary people; a righteousness that is not ours credited to us as though it were; a resurrection body; a new heaven and a new earth; and, at the end of it, his face.

Nobody has ever finished that sentence. The apostles did not, and the church has been trying for two thousand years, and the people who see him will spend eternity discovering how much of it they had not yet understood.

Thanks be to God. There is nothing else to say about a gift like that, and Paul, who could argue for chapters, does not try.

9.text: <sup>1</sup>Now it is superfluous for me to write to you about the ministry for the saints,<sup>2</sup>for I know your readiness, of which I boast about you to the people of Macedonia, saying that Achaia has been ready since last year. And your zeal has stirred up most of them.<sup>3</sup>But I am sending the brothers so that our boasting about you may not prove empty in this matter, so that you may be ready, as I said you would be.<sup>4</sup>Otherwise, if some Macedonians come with me and find that you are not ready, we would be humiliated—to say nothing of you—for being so confident.<sup>5</sup>So I thought it necessary to urge the brothers to go on ahead to you and arrange in advance for the gift you have promised, so that it may be ready as a willing gift, not as an exaction.<sup>6</sup>The point is this: whoever sows sparingly will also reap sparingly, and whoever sows bountifully will also reap bountifully.<sup>7</sup>Each one must give as he has decided in his heart, not reluctantly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver.<sup>8</sup>And God is able to make all grace abound to you, so that having all sufficiency in all things at all times, you may abound in every good work.<sup>9</sup>As it is written, “He has distributed freely, he has given to the poor; his righteousness endures forever.”<sup>10</sup>He who supplies seed to the sower and bread for food will supply and multiply your seed for sowing and increase the harvest of your righteousness.<sup>11</sup>You will be enriched in every way to be generous in every way, which through us will produce thanksgiving to God.<sup>12</sup>For the ministry of this service is not only supplying the needs of the saints but is also overflowing in many thanksgivings to God.<sup>13</sup>By their approval of this service, they will glorify God because of your submission that comes from your confession of the gospel of Christ, and the generosity of your contribution for them and for all others,<sup>14</sup>while they long for you and pray for you, because of the surpassing grace of God upon you.<sup>15</sup>Thanks be to God for his inexpressible gift!

10.title: Divine Weapons and Boasting in the Lord
10.overview:
With chapter 10 the tone of the letter shifts sharply. The warm, reconciling chapters 1–9 give way to the sharp, ironic defence of chapters 10–13, with its “fool’s speech,” in which Paul directly confronts the super-apostles who have infiltrated the Corinthian church and challenged his authority. The shift is so marked that some scholars have argued chapters 10–13 are a separate letter (the “severe letter” of 2:3–4); the majority view is that they are the final section of the same letter, addressed to a minority in the church that is still resistant to Paul.

Chapter 10 opens with Paul’s self-description: meek and gentle in person, bold when away. He addresses the charge that he is weak in person but bold in his letters — a charge that amounts to saying his authority is empty. He does not deny the meekness; he redefines the basis of authority. The weapons of his warfare are not fleshly but divinely powerful for pulling down strongholds, destroying arguments, and taking every thought captive to the obedience of Christ. The battle is not physical or rhetorical; it is spiritual and intellectual.

The chapter closes with one of the most important principles in the letter: the one who boasts must boast in the Lord (v. 17, quoting Jer. 9:24). The super-apostles measure themselves by themselves and compare themselves to themselves — a closed system of self-referential evaluation. Paul’s only standard is the Lord’s commendation: “it is not the one who commends himself who is approved, but the one whom the Lord commends.”

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — The Weapons of Divine Warfare
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul appeals to the Corinthians by the meekness and gentleness of Christ (v. 1) — invoking Christ’s own character as the pattern for his approach, and doing it at the head of four chapters of self-defence, which should govern how all of them are read. He addresses the charge that he is humble in person but bold in letters by reframing the entire question: his boldness, when it comes, will not be directed at the church but at those who suspect him of walking according to the flesh (v. 2), and he would greatly prefer not to have to show it at all.

The warfare he is engaged in is not flesh-level warfare (v. 3); it is a spiritual campaign whose weapons are divinely powerful (v. 4) — the image is siege warfare, which every Corinthian understood, living beneath the fortress on the Acrocorinth. “We destroy arguments and every lofty opinion raised against the knowledge of God, and take every thought captive to obey Christ” (v. 5). This verse is one of the most frequently quoted in discussions of the Christian mind. The arguments and lofty opinions that are raised against the knowledge of God are not merely intellectual errors but spiritual fortifications — the organised resistance of human reason and pride to the self-revelation of God. The ministry of the gospel is not merely persuasion but demolition and reconstruction: tearing down the fortifications and establishing Christ’s lordship over the mind.

Verse 6 completes the siege picture and shows Paul’s timing: he is ready to punish every disobedience — but only when your obedience is complete. He deliberately waits for the body of the church to be settled before moving against the remaining resistance, so that nobody is forced to choose sides prematurely. And he frames the whole affair as obedience to Christ rather than loyalty to himself, which is what keeps church discipline from becoming a power struggle.
verseByVerse.theology: The “weapons of warfare” in v. 4 are the weapons of gospel ministry: the proclaimed word, prayer, the demonstration of transformed lives, the power of the Spirit. These are not powerful by worldly standards (rhetorical brilliance, social influence, political power) but divinely powerful for pulling down strongholds. This is the consistent NT theology of ministry: God chooses the weak and foolish things to shame the strong and wise (1 Cor. 1:27), precisely so that the power is unmistakably his. The church that abandons the means God has ordained in favour of worldly methods of influence has swapped divinely powerful weapons for humanly impressive ones.
verseByVerse.examples: A church in a university town hires a communications consultant to help them “win the argument” with the secular culture. The consultant advises them to lead with culturally acceptable values rather than with gospel claims. This passage challenges the strategy: taking every thought captive to the obedience of Christ is the goal, but the weapons for achieving it are not strategic communication management — they are the divinely powerful weapons of the gospel, prayer, and the demonstration of transformed lives. The strongholds that prevent the knowledge of God are spiritual, and only spiritual weapons can pull them down.

verseByVerse.quote: I, Paul, myself entreat you, by the meekness and gentleness of Christ—I who am humble when face to face with you, but bold toward you when I am away!— I beg of you that when I am present I may not have to show boldness with such confidence as I count on showing against some who suspect us of walking according to the flesh.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I, Paul, myself entreat you, by the meekness and gentleness of Christ — I who am humble when face to face with you, but bold toward you when I am away! — I beg of you that when I am present I may not have to show boldness with such confidence as I count on showing against some who suspect us of walking according to the flesh.

The tone of the letter changes here, and everyone who reads it notices. For nine chapters Paul has been warm, relieved, confident in them. From this verse to the end he is fighting.

Some have concluded that chapters 10 to 13 must be a separate letter stitched on. There is no manuscript evidence for it, and there is a simpler explanation: he has finished with the majority who have come right, and now turns to the minority who have not, and to the men who have been working on them.

I, Paul, myself. The pronouns pile up. He is stepping forward personally, and after this the letter will be full of I where before it was largely we.

And notice what he swears by: the meekness and gentleness of Christ. Before a word of combat he names the character he intends to fight in. Meekness is the word of the Beatitudes and of the Lord’s own self-description — I am gentle and lowly in heart (Matt. 11:29). Gentleness is the quality of a man who does not insist on the full severity of what he is entitled to; it is the word used of a ruler who has the right to press a charge and does not.

That is a remarkable thing to put at the head of four chapters of self-defence, and it should govern how they are read. Whatever sharpness follows is meant to be heard in that key.

Then the taunt, quoted in his own sentence with a note of exasperation: I who am humble when face to face with you, but bold toward you when I am away. They were saying he was brave on paper and small in the room — that he wrote what he did not dare say.

It is an accusation with real force, and it lands somewhere near home for most of us. Almost everyone is bolder at a distance. The message says what the conversation would not. The complaint made in the car is not made in the meeting. The strong opinion typed at eleven at night would be softened considerably by a face on the other side of a table.

Paul’s answer is not to become fierce in person. It is to say that the gentleness they mistook for cowardice was deliberate, and that he would greatly prefer not to have to prove it. I beg of you that when I am present I may not have to show boldness. He is asking them to make the confrontation unnecessary.

That is what strength under control looks like, and it is why he began where he did. Meekness is not the inability to be forceful. It is force with a hand on it — and the man who models it had legions at his disposal and stood silent in front of Pilate (Matt. 26:53; 27:14).
verseByVerse.note: Chapters 10–13 answer rival teachers at Corinth who belittled Paul.

parallels.desc: Moses was very meek

verseByVerse.quote: For though we walk in the flesh, we are not waging war according to the flesh. For the weapons of our warfare are not of the flesh but have divine power to destroy strongholds.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For though we walk in the flesh, we are not waging war according to the flesh. For the weapons of our warfare are not of the flesh but have divine power to destroy strongholds.

They had accused him of walking according to the flesh — of operating by ordinary human motives and methods. He picks the word up and turns it over.

Though we walk in the flesh. Yes, in one sense. He is a man, in a body, with a digestive system and a bad back and a temper to govern. He has never claimed otherwise; six chapters ago he called himself a clay pot.

We are not waging war according to the flesh. That is the different question. Living in a body is not the same as fighting by the body’s rules.

And now the picture that governs the rest of the chapter. Paul reaches for siege warfare, and his readers knew what he meant. Corinth sat under the Acrocorinth, a rock rising nearly two thousand feet above the city with a fortress on top of it. Every Corinthian looked up at it daily. A stronghold was not an idea to them; it was that.

The weapons of our warfare are not of the flesh. Name what fleshly weapons would be in this fight: rhetoric, reputation, credentials, charm, political leverage, the ability to out-argue and out-manoeuvre. Precisely the arsenal Paul’s rivals carried, and precisely what he keeps refusing to pick up.

But have divine power to destroy strongholds. The Greek says the weapons are “powerful to God” — the power is his, lent to the weapons he ordained. What are they? The passage does not list them, but the letter has: the open statement of the truth (4:2), a gospel about a crucified man, prayer, the visible transformation of ordinary lives, and a messenger who is manifestly not the source of the power.

Does this passage license binding demons, praying against territorial spirits, or breaking strongholds over cities? No. The strongholds Paul names in the next verse are arguments and every lofty opinion raised against the knowledge of God: false ideas, not demonic territories. The weapons are the truth of the gospel and prayer. Scripture does speak of spiritual forces of evil (Eph 6:12), but the believer’s part there is to stand, resist and pray, not to name and bind spirits over places.

The uncomfortable question this puts to the church is whether we actually believe it. It is a great deal easier to reach for the fleshly weapons, because they are visible and they work in the short term — the campaign, the polish, the political alignment, the personality who can hold a room. None is wicked in itself. But a church that has quietly swapped divinely powerful weapons for humanly impressive ones will find it has won some arguments and pulled down no strongholds at all.

And the arithmetic runs the other way from what we expect. God chose what is weak in the world to shame the strong (1 Cor. 1:27) — a message about an executed provincial, carried by unimpressive people. That is not a handicap he graciously works around. It is the chosen instrument, and it has been levelling fortresses for two thousand years.
verseByVerse.note: Strongholds were fortified towers or citadels.

verseByVerse.quote: We destroy arguments and every lofty opinion raised against the knowledge of God, and take every thought captive to obey Christ,
verseByVerse.commentary:
We destroy arguments and every lofty opinion raised against the knowledge of God, and take every thought captive to obey Christ,

The siege continues, and now we are told what the fortress is made of.

Arguments — logismoi, reasonings, the constructions the mind builds. And every lofty opinion, literally every “high thing” raised up; the word is used of a rampart, something built tall specifically to keep an enemy out.

Note carefully what these are raised against: the knowledge of God. This is not a description of ideas that happen to be mistaken. It is a description of intellectual structures whose function is to keep God at a distance. And that is worth saying plainly, because it explains something otherwise puzzling. Very often the reasons a person gives for not believing are genuinely held and also not the real reason. They are the wall, and the wall was built for a purpose.

Against these Paul uses two verbs, and both are military. He destroys — pulls down, demolishes. And he takes captive: aichmalōtizō, the word for marching a prisoner of war away at spearpoint. First the wall comes down, then the occupants are led out.

Every thought captive to obey Christ. Every one. There is no province of human thinking with a treaty exempting it.

Now, this verse is quoted constantly, and almost always about the private thought-life — the anxious spiral at three in the morning, the intrusive thought, the resentment rehearsed for the tenth time. That application is legitimate and it is needed; a Christian who lets his mind run wherever it likes is being formed by it. But it is worth seeing that it is a second application rather than the first. Paul is describing his public ministry: the demolition of ideas that stand against the knowledge of God.

How is it done in practice? First, notice the thought for what it is. Then test it against what is true: is it what God says about himself, about Christ and about me? Then replace it, deliberately, with what is true, as Paul says, whatever is true … think about these things (Phil 4:8), and take it to God in prayer. An unwanted thought is not itself sin; it becomes sin when it is welcomed and fed. And where anxious or intrusive thoughts will not go, a believer should not be ashamed to seek help from a pastor or doctor.

Which makes this the most ambitious intellectual programme anyone has ever proposed, and the opposite of the anti-intellectualism it is sometimes made to serve. Paul is not telling people to stop thinking. He is saying that every field of human thought — history, law, art, medicine, economics, the way you read a novel or run a business — is territory Christ intends to hold, and that the Christian mind is not a smaller thing than the unbelieving mind but a conquered and therefore ordered one.

And then there is the personal edge, which no one escapes. Take the strongholds seriously in your own case. Most of us have one — an area where we have quietly built a high wall and decorated it with reasons: the relationship we will not reconsider, the habit that has an argument attached to it, the part of Scripture we have found a way round. It is not that we have never thought about it. It is that all the thinking has gone into the rampart.

Those come down the same way the public ones do, and by the same weapons, and to the same Lord.

verseByVerse.quote: being ready to punish every disobedience, when your obedience is complete.
verseByVerse.commentary:
being ready to punish every disobedience, when your obedience is complete.

The siege image runs on into its last stage, and the order of the sentence is the whole point.

In ancient warfare, when a city fell there was a distinction between the population that submitted and the resistance that fought on. Paul is still inside that picture. The campaign in Corinth is nearly over; most of the city has come in. There remains a pocket that has not, and he says he is ready to deal with it.

But look when. When your obedience is complete. Not before.

He is deliberately waiting. He will not move against the resistance while the majority is still coming over, because action taken too early would force people to choose sides before they were ready and would drive the undecided into the wrong camp. He has done this all through the letter: he stayed away to spare them (1:23), he wrote instead of visiting (2:3), he let the severe letter do its work and waited months for news. Every time, he has given them room and time.

That is patience with a plan behind it, and it is not the same as avoidance. Avoidance hopes the problem will dissolve. Paul is quite clear that he intends to act, and says so in advance, which is itself a mercy — nobody in Corinth can claim to have been ambushed.

There is a real pastoral wisdom here for anyone with responsibility in a church or a family. The instinct when trouble appears is to move immediately and settle it, and the instinct is usually wrong. Timing is not a detail; it is most of the skill. A confrontation that would have split a congregation in March can be handled almost quietly in September, once the body of people has become settled and the issue is no longer a contest between factions.

And notice the two words held together: disobedience and obedience, side by side in one line. Paul frames the whole affair not as loyalty to himself but as obedience to Christ. The Corinthians are not being asked to take his side. They are being asked to submit to the same Lord he is under — which is exactly what he said in 1:24, where he refused to lord it over their faith.

That distinction keeps church discipline from becoming a power struggle, and it is the first thing lost when a leader begins to experience opposition as a personal injury. The question is never “are they with me?” It is whether they are obeying Christ, and the man asking has to be under the same authority, or he has no business asking at all.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
“Look at what is before your eyes” (v. 7) is both a command and a diagnosis: the Corinthians judged by appearance, which is the fault line running through the whole letter. To rivals claiming a special relation to Christ, Paul replies not by denying their claim but by saying that whatever they are, he is too — a very controlled answer from a man who could have said more.

Verse 8 then states the limit on all Christian authority, and it is one of the most important sentences in the New Testament on the subject: the authority is real, it was given by the Lord, and it was given “for building you up and not for destroying you.” The demolition of vv. 4–5 is aimed at strongholds, never at people. Authority used to destroy has ceased to be the thing it was given as.

Paul then addresses the charge directly (vv. 9–10): his opponents say his letters are weighty and strong, but his bodily presence is weak, and his speech of no account. Paul does not dispute the personal weakness — he has already embraced the jar-of-clay theology — and he quotes the insult in the words of the men who made it. But he insists (v. 11) that what he says by letter when absent he does when present: there is no gap between the written man and the man in the room.

The fundamental problem with the super-apostles is their metric of comparison (v. 12): “they measure themselves by one another and compare themselves with one another.” This is a closed loop of self-referential evaluation — setting themselves as the standard, measuring themselves against themselves — and Paul’s verdict is that it is not proud so much as senseless. He refuses the game.

He has been given a particular field of ministry by God (v. 13) — a plot marked out with a surveyor’s rod — and his boasting is limited to that field and to what God has done in it — and Corinth is legitimately in it, because he was the first to come all the way there with the gospel (v. 14). He will not boast beyond measure in other men’s labours (v. 15); his hope is that as their faith grows he will be released to preach where Christ has not been named at all (v. 16), building on nobody else’s foundation.

The governing principle is Jeremiah 9:24, quoted in v. 17: “let him who boasts, boast in the Lord.” This principle is not merely a check on pride; it is a description of the only legitimate ground of ministerial confidence. The approved minister (v. 18) is not the one who commends himself but the one whom the Lord commends. All other forms of self-promotion — however dressed up in spiritual language — are ultimately empty.
verseByVerse.theology: The criterion of the Lord’s commendation (v. 18) is the basis of all genuine ministerial authority in the NT. The super-apostles derive their authority from letters of recommendation (3:1), impressive personal presence, rhetorical skill, and visions and revelations (12:1). Paul derives his from the divine call (Gal. 1:1), the fruit of his ministry (the transformed Corinthians — 3:2), and ultimately from the Lord’s own assessment. This does not make Paul self-certifying; it means his legitimacy is determined at the bar of heaven, not at the bar of human opinion.
verseByVerse.examples: A minister with a large platform cultivates an online presence that constantly showcases his ministry’s results — attendance figures, conversion stories, speaking engagements, endorsements from well-known figures. He tells himself he is building credibility for the gospel. This passage asks a harder question: is he building the gospel’s credibility or his own? The test is not whether he mentions God in his self-promotion but whether his confidence is ultimately in the Lord’s assessment or in the metrics of human comparison.

verseByVerse.quote: Look at what is before your eyes. If anyone is confident that he is Christ’s, let him remind himself that just as he is Christ’s, so also are we. For even if I boast a little too much of our authority, which the Lord gave for building you up and not for destroying you, I will not be ashamed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Look at what is before your eyes. If anyone is confident that he is Christ’s, let him remind himself that just as he is Christ’s, so also are we. For even if I boast a little too much of our authority, which the Lord gave for building you up and not for destroying you, I will not be ashamed.

Look at what is before your eyes. The opening is blunt and slightly weary. It can be read as a command — look at the plain facts — or as a diagnosis: you judge by what is in front of your eyes. Given how much of this letter is about outward appearance against the heart, the second is probably in it, and the first-century Corinthian church had made a habit of the mistake.

Then a sentence with unexpected restraint in it. If anyone is confident that he is Christ’s, let him remind himself that just as he is Christ’s, so also are we.

The rivals evidently claimed to belong to Christ in some special way. Paul’s reply is not “and they do not.” He does not deny their claim; he simply says that whatever they are, he is too. That is a very controlled response from a man who could have said a great deal more, and it is the meekness of verse 1 in operation.

Then verse 8, and the parenthesis in the middle of it is one of the most important sentences in the New Testament about authority in the church.

Our authority, which the Lord gave for building you up and not for destroying you.

Three things are settled in a dozen words. The authority is real — he has it and does not apologise for having it. It is given, not achieved or seized, which means it is held on someone else’s terms. And it has a stated purpose, with a stated limit: it is for construction, and it is not for demolition.

Read that against the verses just before, and the irony is deliberate. Paul has spent four verses on siege warfare, demolishing ramparts and taking prisoners. Now he says his authority is not for destroying. The demolition is aimed at the strongholds; it is never aimed at the people. He tears down arguments in order to build up the person who was living behind them.

Which supplies a test that any Christian in any position of responsibility can apply, and it is uncomfortably simple. After you have exercised authority — as an elder, a parent, an employer, a husband — is the other person more built up or less? Not “were you right?” You may have been entirely right and still have used the truth as a wrecking ball.

Authority given for building up cannot be used to destroy without ceasing to be the thing it was given as. That is the line, and a man who crosses it is no longer exercising the authority Christ gave; he is exercising something else and using Christ’s name for it.

verseByVerse.quote: I do not want to appear to be frightening you with my letters. For they say, “His letters are weighty and strong, but his bodily presence is weak, and his speech of no account.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
I do not want to appear to be frightening you with my letters. For they say, “His letters are weighty and strong, but his bodily presence is weak, and his speech of no account.”

Here Paul quotes his critics directly, and it is the cruellest thing said about anyone in the New Testament that we have in the words of the people who said it.

Take the insult apart, because it was carefully made.

His letters are weighty and strong. That is a concession, and it is the setup. They grant the letters their force in order to make the contrast land harder.

His bodily presence is weak. The word covers appearance and physical bearing. He was evidently unimpressive to look at — small, worn, possibly damaged by the beatings, possibly by whatever the thorn in the flesh was. An early tradition outside the Bible describes him as short, balding and bandy-legged; the tradition is late and cannot be verified, but it survives precisely because nobody in the early church found it surprising.

And his speech of no account. Literally, despised. In a Greek city, public speaking was the highest art and the crowd was expert. Paul was not what they were used to. He had told them so himself in the first letter: he came not with lofty speech or wisdom, and in weakness and in fear and much trembling (1 Cor. 2:1–3).

So the charge is: he can write, but he cannot hold a room, and he does not look like anything. And it worked, because it was substantially true.

Sit with what it must have been to read that sentence aloud, or to hear it read, in the church you founded. He does not answer it with a denial. There is no “that is unfair.” He quotes it, and moves on to the one thing that matters, which is whether the authority is real.

And there is something here for a great many Christians who will never be apostles. Some people are simply not impressive in the way a room rewards. The voice is wrong. The manner is awkward. They think of the right sentence in the car afterwards. They have watched someone with half their faithfulness be listened to twice as attentively, and they have concluded, quietly, that God can use other people.

The most fruitful human being in the history of the church was despised as a speaker and unimpressive in person, and it is recorded in Scripture in the exact words of the men who despised him. God did not correct their assessment. He simply went on using the man they had correctly described — because the treasure was never the jar (4:7), and the power was never going to be mistaken for personality.
verseByVerse.note: Greek culture prized impressive physical presence and polished oratory.

verseByVerse.quote: Let such a person understand that what we say by letter when absent, we do when present.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let such a person understand that what we say by letter when absent, we do when present.

One sentence, and it disposes of the whole accusation.

The charge was a gap between the written Paul and the present Paul. His answer is that there is no gap. What the letters say, the man does. The distance changes nothing.

Notice that he does not promise to be more forceful in person than they expect. He promises consistency, which is a different and larger claim. The letters have been gentle as well as firm — he has begged, entreated, wept and appealed by the meekness of Christ. All of that will also be true in the room. He is not warning them that a harsher man is coming; he is telling them the same man is coming.

Let such a person understand. Singular, and slightly cold. He has a particular individual in view — probably the ringleader of the opposition — and he addresses him without naming him, which is both a courtesy and a warning.

Now the practical force of the verse, because it reaches a very long way past first-century Corinth.

The gap Paul is denying is the commonest failure of integrity there is, and modern life has industrialised it. Almost everyone is now two people: the one who writes and the one who is present. Things are typed that would never be said. A tone is taken at a keyboard that would collapse instantly if the other person were in the chair opposite. Whole reputations are built in a medium where the audience cannot see the man, and the people who live with him could tell you he is not that.

And it runs the other way too, which is the more respectable version. There are people who are warm and agreeable in person and quietly devastating about the same person elsewhere — nothing untrue said, exactly, but a different man in each room.

The test is Paul’s, and it is simple enough to run tonight. Would you be content for the person you wrote about to read what you wrote? Would you say, to their face, the thing you said about them at the kitchen table? If the honest answer is no, the gap is real, and it is the gap his enemies were accusing him of and could not make stick.

Integrity is a word that means undividedness. It is not chiefly about grand honesty in large matters; it is about being one person. And the reason it is worth the cost is that a divided man can be trusted by nobody, including himself — while the man who is the same in the letter and in the room can be believed the first time, every time, which is the only foundation a ministry or a marriage has ever been built on.

verseByVerse.quote: Not that we dare to classify or compare ourselves with some of those who are commending themselves. But when they measure themselves by one another and compare themselves with one another, they are without understanding.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Not that we dare to classify or compare ourselves with some of those who are commending themselves. But when they measure themselves by one another and compare themselves with one another, they are without understanding.

Paul now names what is actually wrong with his rivals, and it is not their doctrine. It is their measuring system.

He opens with heavy irony: he does not dare to put ourselves in the same class as these men. Of course he does not dare. He is not qualified to compete with people who are that impressive — and everyone reading heard the smile in it.

Then the diagnosis, and it is exact. They measure themselves by one another and compare themselves with one another. Follow the circle. They are the standard. They are the ruler and the thing being measured. Nothing external is ever allowed into the calculation, so the result is always satisfactory.

Paul’s verdict on it is blunt: they are without understanding. Not proud, not mistaken — stupid. It is a foolish way to live, in the ordinary sense of foolish, because it guarantees you will never learn anything true about yourself.

And this is where the passage stops being about first-century opponents, because comparison is the water most people swim in and it is worse now than it has ever been.

Think about how it actually operates. You do not compare yourself with everyone; you select. The comparison group is chosen, unconsciously, to produce a tolerable result — near enough to be relevant, and arranged so that you come out somewhere acceptable. And the effect is always one of two things, and both are ruinous.

Either you come out ahead, and you are quietly pleased, and the pleasure is in being better than someone rather than in anything real. Or you come out behind, and something corrosive begins — the diminishment, the resentment of a person who has done you no harm, the sense that your own work does not count. Neither of those tells you a single true thing about yourself, because the measurement never touched the actual standard.

It is worth naming where this bites hardest now. A generation ago a person compared himself with the twenty families in his street. He now compares himself, several times a day, with a curated selection of the most successful, most photogenic and most articulate people on earth, all of whom are presenting their edited version. Nobody has ever had to endure that before, and it is not surprising that so many people feel like failures at something they were never in a contest about.

The way out is not to try harder at the comparison. It is to change the ruler, which is what Paul does in the next six verses, and where he ends is the only place there is: let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord.

verseByVerse.quote: But we will not boast beyond limits, but will boast only with regard to the area of influence God assigned to us, to reach even to you. For we are not overextending ourselves, as though we did not reach you. For we were the first to come all the way to you with the gospel of Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But we will not boast beyond limits, but will boast only with regard to the area of influence God assigned to us, to reach even to you. For we are not overextending ourselves, as though we did not reach you. For we were the first to come all the way to you with the gospel of Christ.

Having refused the comparison game, Paul says what he measures by instead.

The phrase rendered area of influence is a single Greek word, kanōn. It means a measuring rod, and then by extension the boundary marked out with one — the surveyor’s line, the allotted plot. It is the word from which we get canon, the fixed rule.

So Paul’s picture is of a field with boundary markers in it, and the markers were not put there by him: the area of influence God assigned to us. He did not choose the Gentile mission or select Corinth from a list of options. He was given a plot, and he intends to be assessed on that plot and nowhere else.

That single idea disposes of an enormous amount of Christian unhappiness, and it is worth being concrete about how.

If God assigns the field, then the size of your field is not your achievement and not your failure. A man given four acres who works them well has done exactly what a man given four hundred has done, and the accounting at the end will be per acre. So the small congregation is not a lesser version of the large one. The Sunday school class of six is not a failed attempt at sixty. The years given to caring for one dependent relative are not a career that did not happen.

And it works as a restraint as well as a comfort. A man who knows where his boundary markers are does not need to be involved in everything, does not have to have a view on every controversy, and is not obliged to feel guilty about every good work he is not doing. There is a kind of exhausted Christian who is failing at nine things because he was only ever given three.

Then verse 14, and Paul makes the specific claim: he is not overreaching in counting Corinth as his, because we were the first to come all the way to you with the gospel of Christ. He was there before anybody. He crossed from Athens alone, worked at a bench to support himself, and stayed eighteen months (Acts 18:1–11). The rivals arrived later, to a church already standing.

That is the difference between a man on his own ground and a man on someone else’s, and Paul is about to say plainly what he thinks of the second.

verseByVerse.quote: We do not boast beyond limit in the labors of others. But our hope is that as your faith increases, our area of influence among you may be greatly enlarged, so that we may preach the gospel in lands beyond you, without boasting of work already done in another’s area of influence.
verseByVerse.commentary:
We do not boast beyond limit in the labors of others. But our hope is that as your faith increases, our area of influence among you may be greatly enlarged, so that we may preach the gospel in lands beyond you, without boasting of work already done in another’s area of influence.

Now the charge is made explicit, and it is a serious one. The rivals had come to a church somebody else planted and taken credit for it.

We do not boast beyond limit in the labors of others. The image is of a man moving a boundary stone in the night — an old and much-hated crime, forbidden in the Law (Deut. 19:14) — and standing in a field he did not clear, showing visitors round.

It is not a first-century problem only. It happens whenever a man arrives at a work built over thirty years by someone tired and unfashionable, makes some improvements, and lets it be understood that things really began when he came. It happens in the way ministries describe their own history. It is rarely a lie; it is usually a matter of emphasis, and the person who did the clearing is dead or elsewhere and cannot say anything.

Then Paul’s own ambition, and it is worth watching how carefully it is framed.

Our hope is that as your faith increases, our area of influence among you may be greatly enlarged. Notice the sequence. He does not ask for a larger field. He asks that their faith should grow — and expects that his own scope will be enlarged as a consequence, because a church that is spiritually strong releases its workers instead of absorbing them.

So the growth he wants in himself is downstream of the growth he wants in them. That is the right way round, and it is very rarely how ambition is actually ordered. The usual shape is a man wanting a bigger platform and hoping his people will supply it.

So that we may preach the gospel in lands beyond you. There is the aim. He wants Corinth strong so that he can leave. The Corinthians are not his destination; they are a base. And the phrase lands beyond is the sentence of a man who cannot stop looking at the horizon — he tells the Romans he means to go as far as Spain, because he is determined to build on nobody’s foundation (Rom. 15:20–24).

Which is the deepest difference between him and the men troubling this church. They travelled to places where the work was done and the church was gathered. He travelled to places where nobody had heard of Jesus at all. Both are moving; only one is advancing. And the test of any ministry ambition is finally that plain: does it want a share of what already exists, or does it want the gospel to reach somewhere it has not been?
verseByVerse.note: Paul hoped to go on to Rome and Spain.

verseByVerse.quote: “Let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord.” For it is not the one who commends himself who is approved, but the one whom the Lord commends.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord.” For it is not the one who commends himself who is approved, but the one whom the Lord commends.

The chapter ends where the whole argument has been going, and Paul settles it with a quotation.

It is from Jeremiah 9, and the original is worth having in full, because Paul is expecting his readers to hear it: Let not the wise man boast in his wisdom, let not the mighty man boast in his might, let not the rich man boast in his riches, but let him who boasts boast in this, that he understands and knows me (Jer. 9:23–24).

Three things a human being can be proud of — brains, strength, money — and they are still the three. Every comparison anyone runs is finally a version of one of them. Jeremiah does not tell his readers to stop boasting. He tells them to move the object.

That is important, because Scripture is not against boasting as such. Human beings are built to admire and to say so; the instinct is not the problem. The problem is that it keeps attaching itself to things that cannot bear the weight, and that will be gone in fifty years.

Then verse 18, and it is the last word on the subject: it is not the one who commends himself who is approved, but the one whom the Lord commends.

The word approved is the assayer’s word again — tested and found genuine. And the point is about who is holding the scales. A man can commend himself brilliantly and be worthless; he can be despised as a speaker, unimpressive in person, dismissed by the very church he founded, and be approved.

Which is either terrifying or the most liberating sentence in the chapter, depending on where your confidence has been sitting. If your sense of yourself rests on the assessment of the room, this verse takes it away, and there is nothing to be done about that. If it rests on his assessment, then every unfair verdict passed on you is provisional, and the review is scheduled.

And the astonishing thing — the thing that makes this good news rather than merely a warning — is that the commendation Paul is waiting for has already been secured, and not by him. He is approved because he is in Christ, who was made sin for him (5:21), and the words he is waiting to hear will be said over people who know perfectly well they did not earn them.

Let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord. There is nothing else in the universe that will still be worth boasting about when everything currently being compared has been forgotten, and the only opinion that will be left standing is his.

parallels.desc: let him who boasts boast in this

11.title: The Fool's Speech and the Catalogue of Suffering
11.overview:
Chapter 11 contains Paul’s most ironic and self-revealing writing. He embarks on the “fool’s speech” — boasting as the super-apostles boast, but turning the boasting itself into an exposure of their false standards. If they boast in impressive credentials, Paul will boast — in his sufferings and weaknesses, the very things the super-apostles would consider disqualifications.

The chapter opens with Paul’s jealousy for the Corinthians: he has betrothed them to Christ as a pure virgin; he fears they are being led astray from sincere and pure devotion to Christ, just as the serpent deceived Eve. The false apostles are preaching a different Jesus, a different spirit, a different gospel. Paul does not dismiss these as minor variations; he identifies them as satanic counterfeits, presented by false apostles who are servants of Satan disguised as servants of righteousness.

The chapter closes with one of the most remarkable personal disclosures in the NT: Paul’s catalogue of sufferings (vv. 23–29) — more imprisonments, more beatings, near death, five times forty lashes minus one, three times beaten with rods, once stoned, three times shipwrecked, a night and a day adrift at sea — and the inner burden: “there is the daily pressure on me of my anxiety for all the churches.” This is the resume of the authentic apostle, offered as the ultimate rebuttal to those who boast in impressive credentials and spiritual experiences.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–15 — Jealousy for the Corinthians and the False Apostles
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul asks the Corinthians to bear with a little foolishness (v. 1), and explains why he is willing to look ridiculous. His divine jealousy for them (v. 2) — a jealousy with God’s own jealousy — is rooted in his role as their spiritual father: he betrothed them to one husband, to present them to Christ as a pure virgin. The betrothal image is drawn from the Old Testament pattern of God as the husband of Israel (Isa. 54:5; Jer. 3; Ezek. 16), and the role Paul claims is the friend of the bridegroom, who guards the bride until the wedding day.

The comparison to Eve (v. 3) is striking: the serpent did not argue the Corinthians away from Christ with obviously false teaching. He was subtle, crafty, cunning, and what Paul fears losing is not first their orthodoxy but their “sincere and pure devotion to Christ” — the singleness of heart that can be crowded out without anything ever being renounced. The false apostles are preaching “another Jesus,” a “different spirit,” a “different gospel” (v. 4) — not a variation but a different kind of message altogether — and the sting of v. 4 falls on the church: “you put up with it readily enough.”

Verses 5–12 turn to the rivals themselves and to the strangest accusation in the letter. Paul coins a title for them — the “super-apostles” (v. 5) — and concedes the charge of 10:10 without a fight: he is untrained in speaking (v. 6), though not in knowledge. Then the money. He preached free of charge (v. 7), supported by gifts from Macedonia (vv. 8–9), refusing to burden a wealthy church while the poorest churches in the empire paid for his work there. In a patron-client culture that read payment as the mark of a teacher’s worth, this was used against him — and he answers the misreading directly (v. 11): “Because I do not love you? God knows I do!” He will not change the policy (vv. 10, 12), because it is the one piece of evidence his rivals cannot copy without ceasing to be what they are.

The false apostles are not dismissed as misguided enthusiasts; they are identified with Satan (vv. 13–15): “such men are false apostles, deceitful workmen, disguising themselves as apostles of Christ. And no wonder, for even Satan disguises himself as an angel of light.” The most dangerous spiritual deceptions are not the obviously false but the apparently luminous — the ones that look like the genuine article but have substituted a different Jesus, a different spirit, a different gospel. Their disguise of choice is “servants of righteousness,” and their end will correspond to their deeds.
verseByVerse.theology: The identification of false apostles as servants of Satan (v. 15) is one of Paul’s most severe theological statements. It raises the question of how to identify false apostles — since they come disguised as servants of righteousness. The test that Paul has been applying throughout the letter is: what is the content of the message? What is the character of the minister? Does the ministry bear the cruciform pattern of genuine apostolic suffering? Paul’s opponents fail all three tests: their message is a different gospel; their character is self-promotional; their lives show no evidence of the suffering that authentic ministry requires.
verseByVerse.examples: A congregation is attracted to a visiting teacher who is eloquent, radiantly confident, and preaches a message of spiritual empowerment, prosperity, and supernatural experience — all framed in Christian language. The pastor is concerned but cannot point to an obviously heretical statement. This passage gives him the categories: the test is not merely whether Jesus is mentioned but which Jesus is being presented, which spirit is being invoked, which gospel is being preached. The angel-of-light disguise means the most dangerous false teaching often looks impressively spiritual.

verseByVerse.quote: I wish you would bear with me in a little foolishness. Do bear with me! For I feel a divine jealousy for you, since I betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a pure virgin to Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I wish you would bear with me in a little foolishness. Do bear with me! For I feel a divine jealousy for you, since I betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a pure virgin to Christ.

Paul is about to do something he finds distasteful, and he apologises for it twice before he starts. Bear with me in a little foolishness. Do bear with me! The second sentence is almost a plea. He knows how what follows will sound.

Then he explains why he is willing to look ridiculous, and the reason is not wounded pride. I feel a divine jealousy for you. The Greek repeats the root for emphasis — literally, I am jealous for you with God’s own jealousy.

That word needs handling, because jealousy is a vice in most of its ordinary uses and a divine attribute in Scripture. The difference is what is being defended. Envy wants what belongs to someone else. Jealousy of this kind guards what already belongs to you and is being taken. A husband who feels nothing when his wife is being drawn away does not love her more than a jealous man; he loves her less. God calls himself jealous for exactly that reason — the LORD, whose name is Jealous, is a jealous God (Ex. 34:14) — and it is the language of a marriage, not of a tyrant.

Which is precisely the picture Paul now draws: I betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a pure virgin to Christ.

Stage it, because a Jewish betrothal is not a modern engagement. It was legally binding; only a divorce could end it. And there was a role in the proceedings Paul is claiming here — the friend of the bridegroom, who arranged the match, guarded the bride through the betrothal period, and finally presented her to the husband on the wedding day. John the Baptist described himself the same way and said his whole joy was to hear the bridegroom’s voice (Jn. 3:29).

So Paul is not the husband. He is the man who brought the bride to him, and who is responsible for her until the day arrives. That is why he is jealous. Something is happening to his charge on his watch.

Notice what it makes of the church, and it is worth pausing on. This congregation — divided, suspicious, easily impressed by the wrong men — is a bride being kept for a wedding. Everything she is now is provisional. What she is being prepared for is the day she is presented, and Paul’s hope is fixed on how she will look then, not on how she looks this year.

And that is a truer way to see the church than most of us manage. It is not first a society for religious improvement or an institution with problems. It is a woman under an engagement, and the one she is engaged to intends to present her in splendor, without spot or wrinkle (Eph. 5:27). He is coming for her, and he has never once changed his mind about the arrangement.
verseByVerse.note: In a Jewish betrothal the bride was already bound to her husband-to-be, and her purity was guarded until the wedding; Paul pictures himself in that guardian role.
