So the affliction is not the price of the revelation; it is the provision that made the revelation survivable.

Which is worth holding if you carry something that will not go away. The thing you would most like removed may be the thing keeping you usable. It is a hard thought and it is not one to say to anyone else. Paul says it about himself.
verseByVerse.note: No one knows what the thorn was; suggestions include a chronic illness, poor eyesight, or persistent opposition.

parallels.desc: thorns in your sides

verseByVerse.quote: Three times I pleaded with the Lord about this, that it should leave me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three times I pleaded with the Lord about this, that it should leave me.

One line, and it is the verse that keeps a great many Christians in the faith.

Three times. Not a passing mention in his devotions. Three sustained seasons of asking, and the number is probably significant — the Lord himself prayed three times in Gethsemane about a cup he wanted removed (Matt. 26:39–44).

I pleaded. The verb is parakaleō again — the great word of this letter, which has meant comfort throughout and here means to beg. He is not making a polite request. He is imploring.

With the Lord. Worth noticing: Paul’s prayers here are addressed to Jesus, which he does rarely and which tells you something about who he understood him to be.

That it should leave me. Specific, definite, unambiguous. He knew exactly what he wanted and he asked for exactly that.

And the answer was no.

Every element that is supposed to guarantee an answered prayer is present here. The man praying is an apostle. The request is not selfish — a healthy Paul could serve more churches. There is no unconfessed sin, no lack of faith, no failure to persevere; he came back three times. And the thorn stayed.

That has to be said plainly, because a great deal of teaching implies otherwise, and the people it damages are not the strong. There are believers who have been told that healing is theirs if they can muster the faith for it, and who have concluded, after years, that the fault is in them. Some have stopped praying. Some have stopped believing. This verse was written for them. The greatest Christian who ever lived prayed three times for the removal of an affliction and was told no, and the refusal is recorded in Scripture as a mercy rather than a failure.

Notice also that Paul stopped at three. He did not conclude that persistence was the missing ingredient and press on to three hundred. He asked, he received an answer, and the answer settled it. There is a kind of prayer that will not accept a reply, and it is not greater faith; it is a refusal to let God be God.

What changed was not the circumstance but the man, and what changed him was not the passage of time. It was a word — one sentence, given in reply, which he carried for the rest of his life and which the church has been living on ever since.
verseByVerse.note: Jesus too prayed three times in Gethsemane.

verseByVerse.quote: But he said to me, “My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness.” Therefore I will boast all the more gladly of my weaknesses, so that the power of Christ may rest upon me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But he said to me, “My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness.” Therefore I will boast all the more gladly of my weaknesses, so that the power of Christ may rest upon me.

Here is the answer, and it is the summit of the letter.

Begin with the tense, because it is doing more work than any other word in the sentence. My grace is sufficient for you. Not will be, when things get worse. Not has been, looking back. It is sufficient — present, continuous, already true in the moment the thorn is still going in.

The word sufficient means enough, adequate to the need. It is not a promise of abundance or of relief. It is a promise that there will always be exactly as much as is required, and that the supply will not run out before the trouble does.

And notice what was not said. There is no explanation. God does not tell Paul what the thorn is for beyond the one clause of verse 7, does not say how long, does not promise eventual removal. He gives him himself. That is the whole answer.

Then the reason, and it turns the universe over: for my power is made perfect in weakness. The verb is from the root meaning to reach a goal, to be completed. Divine power does not merely cope with human weakness; it comes to its full expression there. Weakness is not the obstacle power has to work around. It is the place power was always heading for.

Guard it from one misreading. This is not a call to cultivate weakness, to refuse medicine, or to make a virtue of incapacity. Paul prayed for removal, three times, and was right to. It means that when the weakness does not lift, you have not been shut out of God’s power. You have been placed exactly where it does its clearest work.

Then Paul’s response, and the word to watch is gladly. Not “I will accept my weaknesses.” Not “I will endure them.” I will boast all the more gladly. Something has been so thoroughly reversed in him that the thing he begged to lose has become the thing he is pleased to have.

And the last phrase gives the reason, and it is worth ending on because it is a picture rather than an argument. So that the power of Christ may rest upon me — the verb means to pitch a tent over. It is built on the word for the tabernacle, where the glory settled in the wilderness, and it shares its root with John’s the Word became flesh and dwelt among us (Jn. 1:14).

So the weakness is not merely tolerated. It is the ground the tent is pitched on. Where a man is emptied out, the glory of God comes down and settles, and stays. That is what the thorn was for, and it is what every unhealed affliction in the life of a believer is being turned to. He did not take it away. He came and lived on it.

parallels.desc: he gives power to the faint

verseByVerse.quote: For the sake of Christ, then, I am content with weaknesses, insults, hardships, persecutions, and calamities. For when I am weak, then I am strong.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For the sake of Christ, then, I am content with weaknesses, insults, hardships, persecutions, and calamities. For when I am weak, then I am strong.

The word to start with is content. The Greek is stronger than the English — it means to take pleasure in, to be well pleased. It is the word the Father uses at the baptism: with whom I am well pleased (Matt. 3:17).

Then five things he is pleased with, and they are not a poetic list. Weaknesses — his own incapacity. Insults — the outrages done to him by people, including the men in Corinth calling him contemptible. Hardships — necessity, the grinding pressure of not enough. Persecutions — being hunted. Calamities — the word means being squeezed into a narrow place with no way out.

Nobody enjoys any of these, and Paul is not claiming to. Notice the qualifier that governs the whole sentence: for the sake of Christ. He does not take pleasure in suffering. He takes pleasure in what the suffering is for and in who meets him inside it. Take Christ out of the sentence and it becomes something unhealthy; leave him in and it is the most liberated sentence in the letter.

That distinction has to be kept, because Christianity has repeatedly produced people who sought out affliction as though the pain itself were holy. It is not. Paul prayed to have his removed. What he learned was not to love the thorn but to love what the thorn made room for.

Then the paradox, stated as flatly as it can be: when I am weak, then I am strong.

It is not a play on words. Both halves are literal, and the then is a hinge — not “although” I am weak but when I am weak, at that moment, precisely there. The strength is not his own returning; it is Christ’s power tabernacling on the empty ground of verse 9.

Which is a genuinely different account of the Christian life from the one most of us carry about. We assume God uses us in proportion to what we bring — that the more competent, the more resourced, the more spiritually together we are, the more useful. This verse says the arithmetic runs the other way at exactly the point where our resources fail.

And it is worth testing against your own history rather than resisting it in the abstract. Think of the times you have been most obviously useful to another person. It is very rarely the season when you were flourishing. It is nearly always the time when you had been through the thing they are going through now, and had nothing to offer but that.

The whole letter has been circling this. The treasure is in clay so the power is plainly God’s (4:7). The captive is the one in the triumph (2:14). The Lord of glory became poor (8:9), and was crucified in weakness — and it is the one event in history that has changed everything.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–21 — Signs of Apostleship and Pastoral Fears
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul closes the fool’s speech with the acknowledgment that he has been a fool to boast (v. 11) — but the Corinthians forced him to it, since they should have commended him and did not. He is not inferior to the super-apostles, even though he is nothing; both halves of that sentence are true at once. The signs of a true apostle were performed among them (v. 12): signs, wonders, and mighty works — but note the phrase attached, “with utmost patience,” which is the qualifier his rivals could not match. The only thing in which they were less favoured than other churches was that he refused to take financial support from them (v. 13), and he asks the ironic question: forgive me this wrong.

He is coming a third time and the policy will not change (v. 14), because “I seek not what is yours but you” — a single sentence that draws the line between a shepherd and a hireling — and because parents save up for children, not children for parents. He speaks now as a father, not as an apostle with terms. Verse 15 is the great statement of pastoral love and of pastoral loneliness in one breath: “I will most gladly spend and be spent for your souls. If I love you more, am I to be loved less?” To spend is to lay out what you have; to be spent is to be laid out yourself, used up — and the adverb is most gladly.

A new accusation surfaces in vv. 16–18: unable to deny Paul’s personal financial integrity, his opponents claim it was a cover for embezzlement by proxy through Titus and the brother sent with him. The very transparency Paul built (8:20–21) has been turned into evidence of a more sophisticated fraud. His answer is not another protestation but a series of questions with names attached — did Titus take advantage of you? did we not take the same steps? — because a public record of consistent behaviour, with witnesses, is the only thing that answers an unfalsifiable charge.

Verse 19 then reframes the whole four chapters: they have not been a defence conducted before the Corinthians at all. “It is in the sight of God that we have been speaking in Christ, and all for your upbuilding, beloved.” The audience is God; the purpose is their construction; and the last word of the sentence — beloved, used here for only the second time in the letter (cf. 7:1) — is the tone the whole passage was meant to be heard in.

The pastoral fears that close the chapter are deeply personal (vv. 20–21). Paul is coming for a third visit, and he fears what he might find — quarrelling, jealousy, anger, hostility, slander, gossip, conceit, disorder: eight relational sins that are the photographic negative of the fruit of the Spirit (Gal. 5:22–23), and every one of them survivable indefinitely by a congregation that would be horrified by anything more obvious. Note the twice-repeated perhaps: he is dreading a possibility, not pronouncing a verdict. And he fears what they might find: a Paul humbled before them, mourning over those who sinned earlier and have not repented. The man who catalogued third-heaven visions in vv. 1–6 is the same man who would weep over unrepentant sin in his congregation — not the administrator worried about institutional health, but the father who grieves over his children.
verseByVerse.theology: The “signs of a true apostle” (v. 12) — signs, wonders, mighty works — are offered not as the primary credential of Paul’s apostleship but as evidence that the Corinthians have already received from him what a true apostle gives. His primary credential, as the entire letter has argued, is the cruciform pattern of his ministry. The miraculous signs are additional evidence, not the foundation. This ordering matters: making miraculous signs the primary criterion for apostolic authenticity is precisely the error of the super-apostles.
verseByVerse.examples: A congregation’s governing board is reviewing the annual ministry assessment and focusing entirely on measurable outcomes — attendance, baptisms, giving — as indicators of pastoral effectiveness. This passage suggests a broader criterion: has the ministry demonstrated the signs of true apostolic work (transformed lives, gospel truth, pastoral care), and has the minister borne the cruciform character that authentic ministry requires? The absence of spectacular growth does not disqualify; the absence of gospel integrity does.

verseByVerse.quote: I have been a fool! You forced me to it, for I ought to have been commended by you. For I was not at all inferior to these super-apostles, even though I am nothing. The signs of a true apostle were performed among you with utmost patience, with signs and wonders and mighty works.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I have been a fool! You forced me to it, for I ought to have been commended by you. For I was not at all inferior to these super-apostles, even though I am nothing. The signs of a true apostle were performed among you with utmost patience, with signs and wonders and mighty works.

The fool’s speech ends, and Paul steps out of the character with obvious relief. I have been a fool!

Then he says whose fault it was: You forced me to it, for I ought to have been commended by you. And that is the real grievance of the whole four chapters. They should have defended him. He founded that church, he was publicly humiliated in it, he was traduced by newcomers — and the people who owed him everything sat quietly. He should never have had to speak.

Anyone who has been left undefended by people who knew better will recognise the note. It is not the attack that wounds most; it is the silence of the ones who could have spoken and did not.

Then the two halves of verse 11, held together without embarrassment: I was not at all inferior to these super-apostles, even though I am nothing.

Both are true and neither cancels the other. Measured against the men impressing Corinth, he is not behind by a step. Measured in himself, he is nothing. That is not self-hatred; it is the settled realism of a man who wrote that our sufficiency is from God (3:5) and that the treasure is in a clay pot. A Christian can hold a very high view of what God has done through him and a very low view of his own contribution, at the same time, without either being false modesty.

Then verse 12, and it is the closest Paul comes to the credentials his rivals traded in: the signs of a true apostle were performed among you… with signs and wonders and mighty works.

So the miracles happened. He does not deny them, and this is one of the plainest statements in the New Testament that the apostles worked them. But look at where he has placed the fact: at the end of four chapters of weakness, mentioned once, in a single line, after the beatings and the basket and the thorn.

Do such signs and apostles continue today? Many Pentecostal and charismatic Christians believe they do, and some speak of modern apostles. But Paul calls these signs the marks of a true apostle, not of every believer, and an apostle had to be a witness of the risen Christ (Acts 1:21–22; 1 Cor 9:1), which Paul says he was Last of all (1 Cor 15:8). The apostles were the church’s foundation (Eph 2:20), laid once. The more likely reading is that the apostolic office and its confirming signs ended with the apostles. God still answers prayer and may heal as he pleases; but the church today is led by elders and taught by the apostles’ words.

And look at the phrase attached to it: with utmost patience. The signs came wrapped in endurance. That is the qualifier his opponents could not match, and it is the one he puts first in the sentence. Power without patience is what they offered. Paul had both, and he lists the patience as the more significant of the two — because anyone can be impressive for an evening, and only a certain kind of man is still there eighteen months later, making tents.

verseByVerse.quote: For in what were you less favored than the rest of the churches, except that I myself did not burden you? Forgive me this wrong! Here for the third time I am ready to come to you. And I will not be a burden, for I seek not what is yours but you. For children are not obligated to save up for their parents, but parents for their children.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For in what were you less favored than the rest of the churches, except that I myself did not burden you? Forgive me this wrong! Here for the third time I am ready to come to you. And I will not be a burden, for I seek not what is yours but you. For children are not obligated to save up for their parents, but parents for their children.

The irony has one more turn in it. In what were you less favored than the rest of the churches, except that I myself did not burden you? Forgive me this wrong!

It is bitter and it is funny, and the sarcasm is aimed at an accusation so absurd that stating it plainly is the best refutation available. The single respect in which Corinth received less than any other church Paul served is that he refused to take their money. He asks their pardon for it.

Then the announcement: here for the third time I am ready to come to you. The first visit founded the church; the second was the painful one; this will be the third. And the policy has not changed and will not: I will not be a burden.

And then the sentence that is the heart of pastoral ministry, and it should be written over every church door: I seek not what is yours but you.

One sentence, and it draws the line between a shepherd and a hireling. The false teachers wanted what the Corinthians had — their money, their allegiance, their admiration, the standing that came from leading a well-known church. Paul wanted the Corinthians. Not what could be got from them. Them.

It is worth running as a test in both directions, because it exposes a great deal. Of anyone who ministers to you: does this person want you, or something you can supply? And of yourself, in whatever relationships you are the stronger party: is it the person you are after, or what they give you — the gratitude, the loyalty, the usefulness, the sense of being needed?

Then the reason, and it changes the whole register: children are not obligated to save up for their parents, but parents for their children.

He has stopped arguing as an apostle and started speaking as a father. And the argument is simply how families work. A father does not present his children with an invoice. The flow of money in a household runs downhill, from the ones who have it to the ones who do not, and nobody regards it as a transaction.

That is how Paul saw his relationship with this difficult, ungrateful, easily-impressed congregation. Not a professional engagement with terms. A family, in which he was the one who paid — which is exactly the position taken by the Father who did not spare his own Son (Rom. 8:32), and who has never once sent anyone a bill.

verseByVerse.quote: I will most gladly spend and be spent for your souls. If I love you more, am I to be loved less?
verseByVerse.commentary:
I will most gladly spend and be spent for your souls. If I love you more, am I to be loved less?

Two sentences. The first is one of the great statements of Christian love; the second is one of the loneliest questions in the New Testament.

I will most gladly spend and be spent. The two verbs are the same root, active and passive, and the difference between them is everything. To spend is to lay out what you have — time, money, energy, effort. To be spent is to be laid out yourself: used up, exhausted, consumed in the process.

Anyone can spend for a while. Being spent is a different order of thing, and it is what actually happens to people who serve others for a long time. They do not merely give things away; they are gradually used up. The mother of a disabled child knows this. So does the man who has cared for his wife through a long decline, and the pastor at year twenty-five.

And the adverb is the astonishing part: most gladly. The superlative. Not “willingly,” not “without complaint.” He is delighted to be used up for them.

For your souls. Not for their approval, their project, or their good opinion. He is spending himself on what will still exist in a thousand years.

Then the question, and Paul lets it stand without answering it: If I love you more, am I to be loved less?

Something has gone wrong that everyone recognises. He has loved them more than any of the newcomers ever will, and it has cost him their affection. The men who exploited them are admired; the man who worked nights so as not to burden them is suspected.

It is a real pain and Paul does not pretend otherwise. But notice that the question does not become a threat or a withdrawal. He asks it, and then goes on loving them and announces he is coming again. Love that stops when it is not returned was something else all along.

And there is only one place this pattern comes from. He came to his own, and his own people did not receive him (Jn. 1:11). The one who loved most was loved least, and was spent entirely, and did it most gladly — for the joy that was set before him (Heb. 12:2) — for people who at the time were shouting for his death. Every servant of his who has loved and not been loved back is standing in a very old and very honourable place.

verseByVerse.quote: But granting that I myself did not burden you, I was crafty, you say, and got the better of you by deceit. Did I take advantage of you through any of those whom I sent to you? I urged Titus to go, and sent the brother with him. Did Titus take advantage of you? Did we not act in the same spirit? Did we not take the same steps?
verseByVerse.commentary:
But granting that I myself did not burden you, I was crafty, you say, and got the better of you by deceit. Did I take advantage of you through any of those whom I sent to you? I urged Titus to go, and sent the brother with him. Did Titus take advantage of you? Did we not act in the same spirit? Did we not take the same steps?

A new accusation, and it is the meanest one yet.

The logic runs like this. Paul’s personal integrity about money could not be denied — he had never taken a penny and the whole province knew it. So the charge mutated. Very well, he did not take it himself; that was the clever part. He was crafty and got the better of you by deceit — meaning that the Jerusalem collection was the real operation, and the money would be siphoned off through the men he sent.

Notice what has happened. The very transparency Paul built — the delegates chosen by the churches, the multiple overseers, the refusal to handle funds alone (8:20–21) — has been turned into evidence of a more sophisticated fraud. That is the nature of a certain kind of suspicion: it is unfalsifiable. Honesty becomes proof of cunning, and precaution becomes proof of something to hide.

Paul’s answer is not another protestation. It is a series of questions with names attached, and that is the only thing that works against an unfalsifiable charge. Did I take advantage of you through any of those whom I sent? Name one. Did Titus take advantage of you? They knew Titus. He had been among them twice; his conduct was a matter of public record and it was spotless.

Then the two closing questions, and they are quietly conclusive: Did we not act in the same spirit? Did we not take the same steps? The word for steps means footprints — walking in the same tracks. Paul and Titus behaved identically about money, and everyone had watched both of them do it.

That is the answer to a whispering campaign, and it is worth knowing because whispering campaigns have not gone out of fashion. You cannot disprove an insinuation by denying it; denial only spreads it. What answers it is a public record of consistent behaviour, and other people who have been seen behaving the same way in the same room.

Which is one more reason for the arrangements of chapter 8. Paul did not build that structure because he expected to be believed. He built it because he expected not to be — and when the accusation finally came, the answer was already in place and had witnesses.

verseByVerse.quote: Have you been thinking all along that we have been defending ourselves to you? It is in the sight of God that we have been speaking in Christ, and all for your upbuilding, beloved.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Have you been thinking all along that we have been defending ourselves to you? It is in the sight of God that we have been speaking in Christ, and all for your upbuilding, beloved.

Paul stops, and reframes the entire four chapters.

Have you been thinking all along that we have been defending ourselves to you? It is the obvious reading, and he knows it; he has spent four chapters answering charges, matching credentials, listing sufferings and refuting accusations. Anyone would call that a defence.

He says it is not — or at least, that they are not the court.

It is in the sight of God that we have been speaking in Christ. There is the correction. He has not been standing in the dock before the Corinthians. He has been speaking with God as the audience, and the Corinthians have merely been in the room.

That single shift changes what all of it was. A man defending himself before people is managing an impression; everything he says is shaped by what will persuade them. A man speaking before God says what is true and lets the impression fall where it will — which is why these chapters contain so much that no advocate would ever have included. No one building a case mentions that he despaired of life, could not rest at Troas though a door was open, is unimpressive in person, and left Damascus in a basket.

And it explains the freedom running under the bitterness. Paul is not frightened of losing the verdict, because the verdict is not theirs to give. He said it at 10:18: the one who is approved is the one the Lord commends.

Then the purpose, and it is the second half of the correction: and all for your upbuilding, beloved.

Every word of it — the irony, the sarcasm, the catalogue of floggings, the fool’s speech he found so distasteful — was construction work on them. Not self-protection. He is back to 10:8: authority given for building up and not for destroying. Even the sharpest chapter in the letter was aimed at making them stronger.

And then the last word of the sentence, dropped in after everything: beloved.

It is only the second time he has used it in the letter (cf. 7:1), and he saves it for here — after four chapters of conflict, addressed to the people who have doubted him, listened to his enemies, and left him to defend himself alone. That is the tone the whole passage was meant to be heard in, and he makes sure they cannot finish it without knowing so.

verseByVerse.quote: For I fear that perhaps when I come I may find you not as I wish, and that you may find me not as you wish—that perhaps there may be quarreling, jealousy, anger, hostility, slander, gossip, conceit, and disorder. I fear that when I come again my God may humble me before you, and I may have to mourn over many of those who sinned earlier and have not repented of the impurity, sexual immorality, and sensuality that they have practiced.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For I fear that perhaps when I come I may find you not as I wish, and that you may find me not as you wish — that perhaps there may be quarreling, jealousy, anger, hostility, slander, gossip, conceit, and disorder. I fear that when I come again my God may humble me before you, and I may have to mourn over many of those who sinned earlier and have not repented of the impurity, sexual immorality, and sensuality that they have practiced.

The chapter ends in fear, and it is worth noticing what Paul is and is not afraid of.

Twice he says I fear, and the first time the word perhaps guards it twice over. He is not predicting; he is dreading a possibility. That small word matters — he has not given up on them, and he will not describe their sin as settled before he has seen it.

Then the list of eight, and read as a group they are not the sins of a pagan city. They are the sins of a church. Quarreling, jealousy, anger, hostility, slander, gossip, conceit, and disorder. Every one of them is a relational sin, and every one is survivable indefinitely by a congregation that would be horrified by anything more obvious. Nobody is disciplined for gossip. Nobody leaves a church over conceit. And these eight are the exact photographic negative of the fruit of the Spirit — love, joy, peace, patience, kindness (Gal. 5:22–23). Where the Spirit is not being followed, this list is what grows in the space.

Then verse 21, and it goes deeper. He is afraid that my God may humble me before you — that he will arrive and find the situation such that he is brought low in front of them. And then the specific dread: I may have to mourn over many of those who sinned earlier and have not repented.

The verb is the strong one — to grieve as at a death. Not to discipline them, though he will; not to be angry, though he might be. To mourn.

And the three sins named are the old Corinthian ones, the things the first letter dealt with: impurity, sexual immorality, sensuality. Some had never actually turned. The letter had been received, the crisis had been resolved, the church had come back to Paul — and underneath it, quietly, a number of people were still living exactly as they had been.

That is a sober note for any church that has come through a good season. Corporate reconciliation is not the same as individual repentance. A congregation can be genuinely restored at the level of its relationships and still contain people for whom nothing has changed at all.

But end where Paul does, on the word mourn. He is not looking forward to the confrontation and he is not sharpening his authority for it. The thought that keeps him awake is that he will have to weep. The apostle of the third heaven, who had been caught up into paradise and heard what may not be repeated, is afraid of arriving in a Greek port and finding people he loves unrepentant — and grieving over them the way a father grieves.

13.title: Self-Examination, Final Warnings, and the Grace Benediction
13.overview:
The final chapter of 2 Corinthians brings the letter to its conclusion with a series of warnings, an extraordinary call to self-examination, and the most famous benediction in the New Testament. Paul announces his coming third visit: “This is the third time I am coming to you. Every charge must be established by the evidence of two or three witnesses.” He will not spare those who have sinned and not repented. He is not weak toward them: Christ is not weak in dealing with them but is powerful among them. The one crucified in weakness was raised in the power of God; Paul, who shares the weakness, also shares the power.

The call to self-examination (vv. 5–6) turns the tables on the Corinthians: they have been examining Paul, demanding proof that Christ speaks in him. Paul says: examine yourselves — test whether you are in the faith. This is not an invitation to doubt but a call to genuine self-knowledge. The Corinthians who know Christ is in them will recognise that Paul too is not disqualified. And Paul’s ultimate desire is not that they recognise his authority but that they do what is right — even if it appears to disqualify him: “We cannot do anything against the truth, but only for the truth.”

The letter ends with the Trinitarian benediction of v. 14 — “the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ and the love of God and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with you all” — the most explicitly Trinitarian formula in the Pauline letters, placing all three persons in coordinate relation and ascribing to each a distinctive gift: grace (Christ), love (God the Father), fellowship (the Holy Spirit).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul’s announcement of his coming third visit (v. 1) carries the legal weight of Deuteronomy 19:15: every charge must be established by two or three witnesses. He is not threatening summary judgment; he is promising due process, in a church where he himself is the injured party. He has given a warning when present the second time; he is giving it again in writing now; when he comes, he will act (v. 2), and the sparing of 1:23 is over.

The Corinthians seek proof that Christ is speaking in him (v. 3), and Paul answers by switching the subject from himself to his Lord: Christ is not weak in dealing with them. The danger being named is real — a church that learns to disregard a gentle minister can slide into disregarding the one who sent him, and end with a domesticated Christ. Verse 4 supplies the theological floor of the whole letter: Christ was crucified in weakness but lives by the power of God; Paul likewise is weak in him, and will live with him by the power of God in dealing with them. The weakness and the authority are both real and both derive from union with Christ.

The call to self-examination (vv. 5–6) is the most important pastoral move in the chapter. Rather than spending more time demanding that the Corinthians recognise his credentials, Paul redirects: examine yourselves. Test whether you are in the faith. The test he suggests is a single question: do you recognise that Jesus Christ is in you? Not whether you are holy enough, or feel enough, but whether he is there. The Greek expects the answer yes, and the failure clause is a sharp afterthought rather than an expectation.

Verses 7–8 then do something extraordinary with the argument. Paul prays that they may do right even if that means he never gets the chance to prove himself and goes on being misjudged — he would rather appear to have failed than have them sin so that he can be vindicated. And he can afford it, because “we cannot do anything against the truth, but only for the truth” (v. 8): his authority is derived from the gospel and functions only in its service, and the truth of God is in no danger from anyone.

The section closes on what he actually wants (vv. 9–10). He is glad to be the weak one provided they are strong — the instinct of a father rather than a rival — and what he prays for is their restoration — the word for mending nets and setting broken bones. That is why the letter was written at all: so that when he comes he may not have to be severe in his use of “the authority that the Lord has given me for building up and not for tearing down.” Every hard sentence in the last four chapters was an attempt to make severity unnecessary.
verseByVerse.theology: The call to self-examination (v. 5) has been used in Reformed tradition as the basis for the practice of self-examination before the Lord’s Supper (1 Cor. 11:28–31). Genuine self-examination is not the cultivation of paralyzing doubt but the honest assessment of the soul before God: am I in the faith? Is Christ in me? Is my trust in Christ or in my own religious performance? The examination that produces assurance is the examination that finds Christ as the ground of hope, not the examination that finds sufficient personal righteousness.
verseByVerse.examples: A congregation prepares for a communion service and the pastor leads a five-minute self-examination period before the elements are distributed. Some members treat it as a routine; others spiral into anxiety. This passage clarifies the goal: not to find sufficient personal holiness to “qualify” for the table, but to find whether Christ is there — whether the faith that receives him is genuine. The person who comes to the table trusting Christ is examining themselves correctly; the person who comes evaluating their performance has missed the point of both the examination and the table.

verseByVerse.quote: This is the third time I am coming to you. Every charge must be established by the evidence of two or three witnesses. I warned those who sinned before and all the others, and I warn them now while absent, as I did when present on my second visit, that if I come again I will not spare them—
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is the third time I am coming to you. Every charge must be established by the evidence of two or three witnesses. I warned those who sinned before and all the others, and I warn them now while absent, as I did when present on my second visit, that if I come again I will not spare them —

The letter turns to business. Paul is coming, and he wants nobody surprised by what happens when he arrives.

He quotes the law: every charge must be established by the evidence of two or three witnesses (Deut. 19:15). It is one of the oldest protections in Scripture — no man is to be condemned on one person’s word — and the Lord himself built it into church discipline (Matt. 18:16).

Why raise it here? Some have read Paul as saying his three visits are the three witnesses, which would be a strange use of the text. The straightforward reading is better: he is telling them that when he comes and deals with the unrepentant, it will be done properly. No summary judgment, no acting on rumour, no apostolic decree from the front. Evidence, witnesses, due process — for people who had been slandering him for a year.

That is worth stopping on. Paul is about to exercise discipline in a church where he has been the injured party, and the first thing he establishes is the procedure that protects the accused. A man who wanted revenge would not begin there.

Then the warning, and notice how carefully he documents it: I warned those who sinned before and all the others, and I warn them now while absent, as I did when present on my second visit. This is the second warning, and he is counting them. He warned them on the painful visit. He is warning them in this letter. Nobody will be able to say they did not know.

That pattern is itself a mercy, and it is how God deals with people. Warnings come before judgment, repeatedly, and they come in time to be acted on. Nineveh got forty days (Jonah 3:4). The generation of the flood got a hundred and twenty years and a man building a boat (Gen. 6:3). Nobody in Scripture is ever ambushed by God.

If I come again I will not spare them. The verb is the one he used at 1:23, where he stayed away to spare them. So the sparing is over. He held off once; he will not hold off twice.

And that answers the charge that has run through the whole letter — that Paul is fierce in his letters and weak in person. The truth was simpler. He had been patient, and they had mistaken patience for inability. It is a very old mistake, and Peter had to answer it about God himself: the Lord is not slow to fulfill his promise as some count slowness, but is patient toward you (2 Pet. 3:9). Delay is not weakness. It is room being given.

parallels.desc: on the evidence of two witnesses or of three

verseByVerse.quote: since you seek proof that Christ is speaking in me. He is not weak in dealing with you, but is powerful among you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
since you seek proof that Christ is speaking in me. He is not weak in dealing with you, but is powerful among you.

Here is the demand behind everything. You seek proof that Christ is speaking in me. The word is dokimē — evidence, the result of a test. They wanted him to demonstrate his authority.

And you can see what kind of demonstration they had in mind, because they had been getting it from somebody else: presence, force, the manner of a man who is plainly in charge. The super-apostles had it. Paul, working nights and declining their money, did not.

The tragedy in the sentence is that they were asking for proof from a man who had given them everything he had. The church itself was the proof (3:2); so were the scars. They were standing inside the evidence and asking to see some.

People do this. A wife who has been loved faithfully for thirty years can still ask whether she is loved, because the thing she is looking for is a gesture rather than a life. The demand for proof is very often a sign that the actual evidence has stopped being looked at.

Then Paul’s answer, and it is a warning dressed as a correction: He is not weak in dealing with you, but is powerful among you.

Notice the switch. They asked about Paul; he answers about Christ. You want to know whether Christ is speaking in me? Then understand what you are asking for. The Christ who deals with you through me is not weak.

There is a real danger being named. A church that has learned to disregard a gentle minister can slide, almost without noticing, into disregarding the Lord who sent him. The messenger’s mildness gets attributed to the message, and then to the one who gave it, and a congregation ends up with a domesticated Christ — endlessly patient in a way that means nothing much is at stake.

Paul will not have it. The gentleness they have experienced is his; the power belongs to someone else, and it is not in short supply.

And that is a genuinely searching thought for anyone who has grown comfortable. If your picture of Christ has quietly become someone who never presses, never confronts and never requires anything, it is worth asking where that picture came from. It did not come from the Gospels, where he cleared a temple with a whip and wept over a city that would not come to him (Jn. 2:15; Lk. 19:41). He is not weak in dealing with his people. He is patient, which is a different thing entirely, and the patience is not infinite in the sense we would like it to be.

verseByVerse.quote: For he was crucified in weakness, but lives by the power of God. For we also are weak in him, but in dealing with you we will live with him by the power of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For he was crucified in weakness, but lives by the power of God. For we also are weak in him, but in dealing with you we will live with him by the power of God.

This is the theological floor under the whole letter, and it is laid in one sentence.

He was crucified in weakness. Take the word at full strength. The crucifixion was not a strategic manoeuvre disguised as defeat; it was defeat. He did not come down. He was held by nails driven by men he had made, mocked by people whose next breath depended on him, and he died the way the powerless die — publicly, slowly, with nothing to show. Weakness is the exact word.

But lives by the power of God. And then the sentence turns, and the turning is the gospel. The same body that hung there is alive. Not a memory kept warm by his followers; alive, by a power that reached into a sealed tomb.

Now watch Paul apply it to himself, and to every servant of Christ since: we also are weak in him, but in dealing with you we will live with him by the power of God.

The pattern is not merely admired; it is shared. Paul’s weakness is not an unfortunate feature of his temperament — it is participation in the weakness of a crucified Lord. And the power he will bring to Corinth is not his own recovered strength; it is resurrection power, belonging to Christ, exercised through a man who has none.

Which finally settles the question the Corinthians could not answer. They had been sorting people into strong and weak and had put Paul in the wrong column. He is telling them the columns do not work, because the one they worship is in both.

And it settles something for anyone who has felt disqualified by their own frailty. The Christian life is not weakness followed by strength, as though the weakness were a phase to get through. It is weakness and power at the same time, in the same person, as it was in Christ himself — crucified in weakness, but lives by the power of God, and both halves are permanently true of him.

Stand back and look at what is being claimed. The centre of the universe is a man who was executed as a criminal and is alive. Everything in the Christian faith runs through that single fact: the forgiveness, the Spirit, the church, the hope of a body that will not fail. There has never been another event like it and there will not need to be. He was crucified in weakness. He lives by the power of God. Everything else in this letter — the clay pots, the thorn, the basket, the beatings — is that one pattern working itself out in the people who belong to him.

verseByVerse.quote: Examine yourselves, to see whether you are in the faith. Test yourselves. Or do you not realize this about yourselves, that Jesus Christ is in you?—unless indeed you fail to meet the test!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Examine yourselves, to see whether you are in the faith. Test yourselves. Or do you not realize this about yourselves, that Jesus Christ is in you? — unless indeed you fail to meet the test!

They had been examining Paul for a year. He turns the instrument round.

The two verbs are deliberate. Examine is peirazō, to put to the test. Test is dokimazō, the word used of assaying metal — heating it to see whether the gold is gold. And both are in the emphatic position, with yourselves placed first in the Greek: yourselves examine, yourselves test.

Now, this verse has done a great deal of damage in the hands of people who have used it to manufacture doubt, so it needs handling with care — because the reader most likely to take it seriously is the one who least needs to.

Start with what the test actually is. Paul supplies it in the same breath, and it is a single question: do you not realize this about yourselves, that Jesus Christ is in you? That is the whole examination. Not “are you holy enough.” Not “is your faith strong enough.” Not “have you felt the right things.” Is Christ there?

And notice the form of the question. It expects the answer yes. Paul is not suggesting they will probably fail; he is confident about them, and he adds the failure clause as a sharp afterthought rather than an expectation. The Greek word for failing the test, adokimos, means what an assayer says of metal that turns out not to be gold at all.

So how is the test run? Look for Christ, not for your performance. Do you love him at all? Do you want to be free of sin, even where you keep losing? Does the gospel still move you? Do you love his people, including the difficult ones? Is there anything in you that was not there before, that you did not put there? None of these is a measure of how well you are doing. Every one of them is a question about whether he is present.

The church has often applied this verse to the Lord’s Supper, where Paul says, Let a person examine himself, then, and so eat (1 Cor 11:28). The examination is not whether you are worthy enough to come; no one is. It is whether you are trusting Christ and willing to turn from your sin. Those who find Christ in them come to the table; the examination is meant to bring them there, not to keep them away.

And here is the reassurance the anxious reader needs, said plainly. Nobody who is genuinely without Christ lies awake worrying about it. The very fear that you might fail this test is itself evidence of a heart that has been made alive — the dead do not check their own pulse. If you are troubled by this verse, it was not written to trouble you.

Which is why the examination, done properly, ends in relief rather than dread. You look inward, find very little to be proud of, and then find Christ there — not because you have kept hold of him but because he has taken up residence and has no intention of leaving. That is what the test is for. It sends you back to the only ground of assurance there has ever been, and it is not you.

verseByVerse.quote: I hope you will find out that we have not failed the test. But we pray to God that you may not do wrong—not that we may appear to have met the test, but that you may do what is right, though we may seem to have failed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I hope you will find out that we have not failed the test. But we pray to God that you may not do wrong — not that we may appear to have met the test, but that you may do what is right, though we may seem to have failed.

Verse 6 sounds like the return of the argument: if you examine yourselves and find Christ in you, you will discover that the man who brought him to you is genuine after all.

And then verse 7 does something extraordinary with it.

We pray to God that you may not do wrong. That is what he actually wants. Not vindication — their obedience. And he goes further, in a sentence that ought to be read twice by anyone in ministry: not that we may appear to have met the test, but that you may do what is right, though we may seem to have failed.

Follow what he is saying. If the Corinthians repent before he arrives, Paul will never get to demonstrate his authority. The showdown will not happen. His critics will go on saying he is all letters and no presence, and there will be nothing he can do about it — because the crisis that would have proved him will have evaporated.

And he prays for exactly that outcome. He would rather be permanently misjudged than have them sin so that he can be proved right.

Sit with how rare that is. Most of us, in a dispute, want two things: for the other person to do right, and for our position to be publicly established. We would not admit that the second matters much, but it does, and it shows up in a small reluctance to let the matter resolve quietly. There is a part of us that needs the wrong to be visible before it is put away.

Paul cuts that off at the root. He puts their good so far ahead of his reputation that he prays away his own vindication.

Take any grievance you are currently carrying and put this to it. Ask honestly: if this were resolved tomorrow, quietly, with no one ever knowing you had been in the right — would you be glad? If the answer is no, or not entirely, then something other than the other person’s good is at work, and it is worth naming.

And notice where Paul is able to leave the matter, because it is the only place it can safely go. He does not need the record corrected, because the record is not kept by the Corinthians. He said it at 10:18: it is not the one who commends himself who is approved, but the one whom the Lord commends. A man who genuinely believes that can afford to look like a failure.

verseByVerse.quote: For we cannot do anything against the truth, but only for the truth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For we cannot do anything against the truth, but only for the truth.

A short verse, and one of the most freeing sentences Paul ever wrote.

Read at the surface it is a statement about Paul’s own limits. His authority is not a possession he may use as he likes; it was given for one purpose and it does not function for any other. If the Corinthians are in the right, he cannot act against them — not “may not,” but cannot. The instrument does not work in that direction.

That is the principle of all ministerial authority and it is worth stating plainly, because its abuse is a running sore in the church. A minister’s authority is derived. It comes from the truth of the gospel and it extends exactly as far as the gospel does and no further. The moment it is used to defend something the gospel does not teach, or to protect a man rather than serve a people, it has stopped being authority at all. There is no such thing as legitimate power in the church exercised against the truth.

So the practical test for anyone under a leader is not “does he have authority?” Very possibly he does. It is “what is he using it for?” Authority spent on truth is real however gently it is exercised. Authority spent on anything else is a costume.

But there is a larger reading in the sentence too, and Paul’s wording invites it. Nobody can do anything against the truth. Not his opponents, not the super-apostles, not the men who have spent a year telling this church that its founder is a fraud.

Take that as a plain statement about the world and it changes how a Christian holds a losing argument. The truth of God is not fragile. It has been attacked in every century by better minds than the ones currently attacking it, and it has buried them all. It does not depend on being defended well, or on the reputation of the people who happen to be carrying it, or on whether this particular church in this particular year believes it.

Which means the worst that can happen to a faithful person is that he is misunderstood for a while. The truth is not at risk. Gamaliel, of all people, saw it: if this plan or this undertaking is of man, it will fail; but if it is of God, you will not be able to overthrow them (Acts 5:38–39).

Nothing has ever been done against the truth. Every attempt has been absorbed and turned, and the greatest attempt of all — the one that killed the Son of God on a Friday — turned out on the Sunday to have been the truth’s own method all along.

verseByVerse.quote: For we are glad when we are weak and you are strong. Your restoration is what we pray for.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For we are glad when we are weak and you are strong. Your restoration is what we pray for.

The word glad is not resignation. It means to rejoice, and Paul says he does it when we are weak and you are strong.

He has been arguing for four chapters that he is not weak, that he is not inferior to the super-apostles, that Christ is powerful in him. And here he says he is delighted to be the weak one, provided they are strong.

That is what a father says. There is no competition in it at all. A parent who has spent himself raising children and watches them outgrow him does not feel diminished; the whole point was to be surpassed. Paul has been spending and being spent (12:15), and the only outcome he wants is a church standing on its own feet.

It is worth measuring ourselves against, because the opposite instinct is very common in Christian work and it is rarely admitted. There is a way of helping people that keeps them slightly dependent — the counsellor whose people never quite graduate, the leader who cannot delegate, the parent who needs to be needed. It looks like devotion and it is a subtle form of self-service, and the tell is exactly this: whether you are genuinely glad when they no longer require you.

Then the word he uses for what he prays for: restoration. The Greek is katartisis, and it is a rich word. It is used of mending nets — the disciples were katartizontes their nets when Jesus called them (Mk. 1:19). It is used of setting a broken bone. It means putting something back into working order so that it can do what it was made for.

That is a better picture of what God does with a damaged church, or a damaged Christian, than most of the ones we carry. Not replacement. Not papering over. Mending — the patient work of joining what has come apart so the thing functions again. A mended net still shows where it tore, and it holds fish.

And it is the same word Paul will use as a command two verses later: aim for restoration. So he prays for the mending and then tells them to work at it, which is how Scripture almost always handles the relationship between God’s work and ours. He asks God for the very thing he then asks them to do, and neither request cancels the other.

verseByVerse.quote: For this reason I write these things while I am away from you, that when I come I may not have to be severe in my use of the authority that the Lord has given me for building up and not for tearing down.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For this reason I write these things while I am away from you, that when I come I may not have to be severe in my use of the authority that the Lord has given me for building up and not for tearing down.

Paul explains, at the end, why the letter exists. It is a piece of pastoral strategy and it is worth seeing clearly.

He writes while I am away so that he will not have to be severe when he is present. The sharpness of the last four chapters is a deliberate attempt to make sharpness unnecessary later. Every hard sentence in this letter was written in the hope that it would spare them a harder conversation.

That reverses the accusation of 10:10 completely. They had said he was bold at a distance and feeble in person. In fact he was bold at a distance so that he would not have to be severe in person — which is not cowardice but mercy, and it is a good deal harder to do than simply arriving and dealing with everyone.

There is a lesson in the method for anyone who has to confront somebody. Say it early, and say it in a way that gives the other person room to move before you are face to face. A warning that arrives in time to be acted on is a kindness; the same words delivered at the confrontation are just a verdict. Paul has now warned them twice (v. 2), and each warning was an attempt to make the visit unnecessary.

Then the phrase that governs everything: the authority that the Lord has given me for building up and not for tearing down.

He has said it before at 10:8, and he repeats it here at the close because it is the charter of all Christian authority. It was given. It has a stated purpose. And the purpose is construction.

Which supplies the plainest test there is for any exercise of power in a church. Not whether the person has the right — they may well. Ask what is being built. Discipline that aims at restoration is building; the same discipline aimed at establishing who is in charge is demolition, and the words used may be identical.

The language reaches back a long way. God told Jeremiah he was appointed to pluck up and to break down… to build and to plant (Jer. 1:10) — and even there, the tearing down served the planting. Nothing in God’s hands is destroyed for its own sake.

And that is why an apostle who could have arrived and imposed order wrote a letter instead, and wept over it, and sent a friend across a sea with it, and waited. He was building.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–14 — Final Greetings and the Trinitarian Benediction
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Paul closes with a rapid series of imperatives (v. 11): rejoice, aim for restoration, comfort one another, agree with one another, live in peace — and then the promise: the God of love and peace will be with you. Each command answers something that had gone wrong in Corinth, and two of them are the letter’s own great words returning. Aim for restoration is the mending of v. 9, now handed to them as work. Comfort one another brings back the great word of chapter 1. And God is named by precisely what that congregation lacked: the God of love and peace.

The holy kiss (v. 12) is not a throwaway. In a Corinthian gathering it crossed every line the city cared about, and the greetings of all the saints (v. 13) remind a troubled congregation that it is not alone.

The final benediction (v. 14) is the most explicitly Trinitarian formula in the Pauline letters: “The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ and the love of God and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with you all.” Each person of the Trinity is named; each is given a distinctive gift.

Grace is attributed to the Lord Jesus Christ — the undeserved favour that flows from his person and work, and the pressure point of this whole letter (8:9; 12:9). Love is attributed to God the Father — the initiating, originating love that sent the Son, standing behind the grace rather than being produced by it (Jn. 3:16; 1 Jn. 4:10). Fellowship is attributed to the Holy Spirit — the participation in the divine life, and the communion with one another, that the Spirit creates and sustains. And the last three words divide nothing: with you all — the loyal and the resistant, the repentant and those Paul expected to have to mourn over, under one undivided blessing.
verseByVerse.theology:
The benediction is not a formula but a theology: it presents the three persons in distinct but coordinated action, each contributing uniquely to the believer’s life. The order (Christ, Father, Spirit) is unusual — the more common Pauline order puts the Father first — possibly because the letter’s concerns have centred on the grace of Christ (the atonement of ch. 5, the self-giving of ch. 8). The coordinated action of all three persons in the single benediction is an implicit trinitarian claim: to receive grace, love, and fellowship from these three distinct persons is to receive from one God in three persons.

Koinōnia of the Holy Spirit — three possible meanings, all theologically valid: (1) the fellowship that the Spirit creates among believers; (2) participation in the Spirit — sharing in the Spirit’s life; (3) the Spirit as the one who communicates fellowship with the Father and Son. These are not mutually exclusive; the Spirit’s work achieves all three simultaneously. Those who are indwelt by the Spirit share in the divine koinōnia — the mutual love and life of the Trinity — and that sharing is expressed in genuine community with one another.
verseByVerse.examples: A church that closes every service with this benediction has been pronouncing it for decades as a familiar liturgical ending. A new pastor stops before pronouncing it and asks the congregation: do you know what you are about to receive? Each phrase is unpacked slowly — the grace that flows from Christ’s cross, the love that originated in the Father’s heart before creation, the fellowship that the Spirit creates both with God and among the gathered community. The familiar words suddenly land with the weight they have always carried. The benediction is not a farewell; it is a sending into the world with the fullness of the Triune God.

verseByVerse.quote: Finally, brothers, rejoice. Aim for restoration, comfort one another, agree with one another, live in peace; and the God of love and peace will be with you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Finally, brothers, rejoice. Aim for restoration, comfort one another, agree with one another, live in peace; and the God of love and peace will be with you.

The tone changes entirely, and the first word out of him is brothers. After a whole letter of defence, irony and warning, that is what he calls them.

Then five imperatives, fired off quickly, and each one answers something that had gone wrong in that church.

Rejoice. The word can also mean farewell, and both senses are probably here. But given the letter it closes, take it as the command: rejoice. Said to a congregation that has been quarrelling, suspicious and divided, and by a man who has been flogged five times.

Aim for restoration. The same word he prayed for in verse 9 — katartizesthe, be mended. What he asked God to do he now tells them to work at. Mend the nets. Set the bone.

Comfort one another. And there is the great word of the letter one last time — parakaleisthe, the word from chapter 1, where God is the God of all comfort who comforts us so that we may be able to comfort others. The letter that opened with comfort coming down from God closes with comfort moving sideways between believers. That is where it was always meant to end up.

Agree with one another. Literally, think the same thing. Not uniformity of opinion — Paul, of all people, was not asking for that. It is the shared mind of people pulling in one direction, which is exactly what a church loses first when it starts sorting itself into parties.

Live in peace. The plainest of the five, and the hardest.

Then the promise, and notice that it comes last rather than first: and the God of love and peace will be with you.

The order matters. He does not say God will be with you and then you will manage these things. He commands the five, and attaches the promise to them. Not because obedience earns God’s presence, but because a church living in mutual comfort and peace is a church where his presence is felt, and a quarrelling one is not — whatever is true of it in principle.

And the title is chosen for them: the God of love and peace. Both nouns are precisely what that congregation lacked. Whatever a church is short of, Paul has a habit of naming God by it at the end of a letter — because the supply was never going to come from inside the room.

verseByVerse.quote: Greet one another with a holy kiss. All the saints greet you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Greet one another with a holy kiss. All the saints greet you.

Two short lines, and it would be easy to skip them. They are doing more than they look.

Greet one another with a holy kiss. Paul gives this instruction in four letters, so it was not a throwaway. In that world a kiss on the cheek was the ordinary greeting between family members and close friends — the equivalent of a handshake or an embrace now, and carrying the same social information: this person is one of mine.

What makes it worth a command is who was doing it to whom. In a Corinthian gathering the kiss crossed every line the city cared about. A slave greeted his owner. A labourer greeted a householder. A Jew greeted a Greek. Outside that room none of those things happened, and inside it they happened weekly, in public, as a matter of course.

And Paul is telling this particular church to do it — the one that had been sorting itself into factions, taking each other to court, and humiliating the poor at the Lord’s table. The instruction has teeth. It is very difficult to greet someone as family in front of the congregation while carrying a grudge against them, which is presumably part of the point.

The word holy is the guard on it. The gesture was to be genuinely a family greeting and nothing else — a caution that was evidently needed then and would be needed now.

Cultures differ, and the form is not the command; a church that shakes hands or embraces is not disobeying. But the substance is not optional, and it is easily lost. A congregation can hold sound doctrine and never once make physical, public, unembarrassed contact across the lines its society draws — and something the New Testament assumed would be visible every week has quietly disappeared.

Then: All the saints greet you. Paul is writing from Macedonia, and he sends greetings from believers the Corinthians have never met — the churches of Philippi and Thessalonica, poor and afflicted, the ones who had funded his work in Corinth.

It is a small line and it does something large. It reminds a troubled congregation, at the very end, that they are not alone and not the whole story. There are Christians across the sea who pray for them, whose names they do not know. The church has never been the size of the room you are standing in.
verseByVerse.note: A kiss was a common greeting between family members and friends.

verseByVerse.quote: The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ and the love of God and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with you all.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ and the love of God and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with you all.

The letter ends here, and it is the fullest benediction in the New Testament — three persons, three gifts, one sentence.

Paul closes his letters with grace, always. Here alone he opens the blessing out into all three, and it is worth asking why this letter. Because every one of the three has been the subject of it. Grace was what he was told was sufficient. Love was what he was accused of lacking. Fellowship was what had broken down between him and them.

The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ. Named first, which is unusual — the Father normally comes first in Paul. But grace has been the pressure point of the whole letter, and this church knows what he means by it: though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor (8:9); my grace is sufficient for you (12:9). It is favour to people who have earned the opposite, and it is the door everything else comes through.

And the love of God. The Father’s love, and it stands behind the grace rather than being produced by it. This is important and often muddled: Christ did not persuade a reluctant Father to love us. The love came first and sent him — in this is love, not that we have loved God but that he loved us and sent his Son (1 Jn. 4:10).

And the fellowship of the Holy Spirit. Koinōnia — sharing, participation, having something in common. It means at least two things and probably both: the Spirit is the one who gives us a share in God himself, and he is the one who makes a collection of unrelated people into a body. Which is precisely what this church needed.

Then the last three words, and they are the most striking in the sentence: with you all.

All of them. The ones who had stayed loyal, and the ones who had listened to his enemies. The man who had insulted him publicly. The people who had let it happen and said nothing. Those who had not yet repented, whom he expected to have to mourn over. Paul has one blessing and he does not divide it.

And there is where the letter comes to rest. It began with a man who had despaired of life itself and found God to be the Father of mercies; it has gone through tears and floggings, a thorn that was never removed, a church that broke his heart and mended, and an apostle lowered out of a window in a basket. It ends with the Triune God pronounced over the whole difficult congregation without distinction.

The grace of the Son, who became poor. The love of the Father, who did not spare him. The fellowship of the Spirit, who makes it ours. Three, and one, and given away freely to people who could never have earned any of it — which is what he has been like from the beginning, and what he will be found to be when everything currently visible has finished happening.
verseByVerse.note: This blessing names Father, Son and Holy Spirit together, and is still widely used to close Christian worship.

parallels.desc: the priestly blessing

13.text: <sup>1</sup>This is the third time I am coming to you. Every charge must be established by the evidence of two or three witnesses.<sup>2</sup>I warned those who sinned before and all the others, and I warn them now while absent, as I did when present on my second visit, that if I come again I will not spare them—<sup>3</sup>since you seek proof that Christ is speaking in me. He is not weak in dealing with you, but is powerful among you.<sup>4</sup>For he was crucified in weakness, but lives by the power of God. For we also are weak in him, but in dealing with you we will live with him by the power of God.<sup>5</sup>Examine yourselves, to see whether you are in the faith. Test yourselves. Or do you not realize this about yourselves, that Jesus Christ is in you?—unless indeed you fail to meet the test!<sup>6</sup>I hope you will find out that we have not failed the test.<sup>7</sup>But we pray to God that you may not do wrong—not that we may appear to have met the test, but that you may do what is right, though we may seem to have failed.<sup>8</sup>For we cannot do anything against the truth, but only for the truth.<sup>9</sup>For we are glad when we are weak and you are strong. Your restoration is what we pray for.<sup>10</sup>For this reason I write these things while I am away from you, that when I come I may not have to be severe in my use of the authority that the Lord has given me for building up and not for tearing down.<sup>11</sup>Finally, brothers, rejoice. Aim for restoration, comfort one another, agree with one another, live in peace; and the God of love and peace will be with you.<sup>12</sup>Greet one another with a holy kiss.<sup>13</sup>All the saints greet you.<sup>14</sup>The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ and the love of God and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with you all.
